speaker: Gerrit W. Gong
title: Come to the Lord in His Holy House
content:
Welcome to conference!
Why did the temple workers cross the road? To help the people on the other side.
In a world of commotion, contention, and cares, the Lord invites us to a place of spiritual safety, harmony, and holiness—the house of the Lord.
There He teaches us His plan of happiness. He endows and blesses us. He prepares us to come home.
In our day, the Lord is bringing His holy house and covenant blessings closer to our homes and hearts. Foundational doctrine can deepen our love for the Lord. It can increase our understanding of the temple and personal temple culture.
First doctrinal foundation: Heavenly Father’s work and glory is for us to return to Him, united as families, happy and forever.
Temple marriages are meant to last forever. Covenant belonging unites a husband, wife, and children, not until death do we part, not until convenience or attraction fade, but by covenant commitment, sacrifice, and consecration. Consistent spiritual nourishment through prayer, scripture, church attendance, service, etc. blesses and sanctifies our marriages and relationships.
Second doctrinal foundation: moral agency. The morning stars sang for joy. We chose God our Father’s loving plan to learn by our own experience. Jesus Christ redeems us from sin, physical death, and spiritual separation.
God’s redeeming work is majestic in its sweep and reach. As the Prophet Joseph Smith saw in vision, every person, except a very few, is saved in a kingdom of glory. We can inherit a glorified, paradisiacal earth and live in the highest degree of celestial glory with God our Father and Jesus Christ.
Agency means we choose, directly and indirectly, our relationships. God will not require a woman or man to be sealed or live in an eternal relationship he or she does not choose.
Agency, faith and repentance, and Jesus Christ’s Atonement make change and forgiveness possible. As we become new creatures in Jesus Christ, we sweeten our relationships. Temple service evokes our Savior’s Atonement. It softens hearts on both sides of the veil.
We find hope and healing when we perform temple ordinances for family members with whom we may earlier have had difficult relationships. Jesus Christ can help us mend, forgive, move forward. We exclaim: “When I did the temple work for my family member, my heart softened.” “I could forgive.” “I was freed.” “Anger and bitterness left.” “I felt peace for the first time.” We may even come to desire sealing with those family members.
Rich blessings await. Please “do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end.” Please do not deliberately delay the spiritual peace and joyful freedom Jesus Christ wants you to have now.
Third doctrinal foundation: When the Holy Spirit of Promise witnesses and confirms the efficacy of ordinances and covenants, they become binding in time and eternity. In His sacred role as Holy Spirit of Promise, the Holy Ghost “witnesses to the Father that the saving ordinances have been performed properly and that the covenants associated with them have been kept.”
As we honor our covenants, the Holy Spirit of Promise seals our relationships with “efficacy, virtue, [and] force.” They are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
In contrast, we would not expect ordinances and covenants we do not honor in faith or action, do not choose or desire, or perhaps even disregard or mock to be binding upon us on earth or in heaven.
With this doctrinal foundation, let us consider five elements of personal temple culture.
First, a temple dedication is a beginning. We are naturally excited when a temple is announced, groundbreaking and construction occur, and dedication takes place. Each is a milestone.
But please, while we are grateful our temples and everything in them are physically beautiful, let us celebrate and treasure even more the spiritual blessings temples bring.
President Dallin H. Oaks exercises all priesthood keys on earth, including keys pertaining to temples. Next Sunday, I am assigned to dedicate the Miraflores Guatemala City Temple. This year, across the world, we anticipate the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles will dedicate 21 temples and rededicate 1 temple.
Second, over the years, when temples were distant, faithful members sacrificed to be sealed in the temple. Some members could come to the temple only once or twice in their lives. In some cases, once in a year.
Today, as temples come closer in many places, we can manifest the precious spirit of temple sacrifice in new ways. We can come to the temple more often. We can search and bring more family names to bless deceased loved ones. As the seasons of our lives allow, we can regularly serve in the Lord’s house, both as temple patron and as temple ordinance worker.
Third, while each temple uniquely fits its place, culture, and circumstance, everything in each temple testifies of Jesus Christ. Temple leaders unitedly love the Lord and focus on temple patrons and workers. In each temple, by authority and in the name of the Lord, ordinances and covenants are truly and faithfully performed and properly recorded. When patrons do their best, our service is acceptable to the Lord.
Fourth, temple sacrifice and temple service include a spirit of gratitude. I mention this with great respect and love. On occasion, a few members may think attending the temple is a right or entitlement rather than a sacred privilege and may be impatient or not understand when assistance comes slowly or is less than they want.
On occasion, some members may feel a temple is smaller or less ornate than they expected. I once heard, “Elder Gong, we are happy to have a temple but sorry it is a small temple.”
I said, “Dear brother, dear sister, ordinances are not big or small. Covenants are not big or small. Please let us never speak of a temple as big or small, elaborate or plain. Let us always only speak with love and gratitude for ‘Holiness to the Lord, the House of the Lord.’”
Please, dear brothers and sisters, wherever we live, let us always be grateful for the gifts of eternity sacred temples bring. Look for the miracles. New converts sometimes testify family on the other side of the veil led the missionaries to find and baptize family on this side of the veil so their family could be united.
Some new converts feel alone. But you are part of Heavenly Father’s family. And when you take family names to the temple, your eternal family extends on both sides of the veil. My father and mother joined our Church as the only members in either of their families. Today, family history and genealogy help connect many Gong and Char family generations. Whatever generation you are in the Church, in the chain of your eternal family, please be a strong link.
Fifth, where possible, please consider saving for and buying your own ceremonial temple clothes—cap or veil, robe, sash, and apron. As we reverently care for and use our own temple clothes, our children and grandchildren can see we love the Lord and our temple covenants.
I know a family of modest means. At their widowed mother’s request, the children saved and purchased their mother her own ceremonial temple clothes. Their mother loved using her own temple clothing as she regularly attended the temple for many years. When their mother passed away, the family honored their mother’s request by burying her in her temple clothes. Their dear mother was ready to enter eternity prepared for the glorious Resurrection.
Dear brothers and sisters, come worship and rejoice with the Lord in the house of the Lord, in temple doctrine and in your own personal temple culture.
So, why did the temple workers cross the road? So God and temple ordinances can protect, bless, and inspire; bring forgiveness, healing, and peace; and unite loved ones here and away. May these blessings of eternity be ours in even greater abundance, I pray, in the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Tamara W. Runia
title: The Sculpting of Our Souls
content:
I love fixing things. If there’s a knot in a shoelace or a necklace, it’s my job to untangle it. I’m also good at stain removal. I see it as a challenge; in fact, some have referred to me as “the stain whisperer.”
It’s human nature to want to fix things—and to become frustrated when something comes along that we cannot fix.
Thirteen years ago our oldest son, Ryan, woke up on a Monday morning, kissed his wife and four young children goodbye, and left for work. A few hours later, he collapsed and died from undetected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. His heart simply stopped.
The next day was his two-year-old daughter Piper’s birthday. As we lit candles on her cake and began to sing, she was looking for her dad, and I realized this was something I would not be able to fix.
Let’s focus on a scripture that has changed the lens through which I view my life. The setting is a jail cell, where Joseph Smith is pleading with God for a reprieve—for a break from his circumstance. Instead, he was told, “All these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.”
I’ve often wondered if the Prophet had any idea when he received this revelation what these words would mean to so many of us now who are also turning to God, pleading for a break.
God’s answer implies that experience is valuable, and I’m learning the only way to get it is to go through it. Can’t we skip over it? Is there some other way? No, there isn’t another way.
It’s like we heard these lessons in a premortal classroom. We studied it there, and we’re living it here, in this laboratory of life. This is where we “put on Christ.”
C. S. Lewis explained, “God intends to give us what we need, not what we now think we want.” But sometimes we’re puzzled when we get what we need, aren’t we? How can our loving Father in Heaven watch as we go through heartbreaking experiences? I’ve wrestled with this, and maybe you have too.
And while I know earth life is about experience, why am I so surprised every time I experience it? Maybe it’s because I grew up hearing things like “If you keep the commandments, you’ll be blessed. Pay your tithing, and the windows of heaven will open. Follow the Word of Wisdom, and you’ll have health and protection.” True promises, right?
So the gospel felt like a big umbrella I could hold over my head to keep the rain from falling on me. But I’ve learned from experience that we’re all going to get rained on. And sometimes we’re going to get pelted!
The gospel isn’t the umbrella; it’s the solid rock we’re standing on during the storm—that “sure foundation … whereon if men build they cannot fall.”
When an angel asked Nephi, “Knowest thou the condescension of God?” he humbly answered, “I know that he loveth his children; nevertheless, I do not know the meaning of all things.”
God’s love has moved me from questions that begin with “why” to reflections that begin, “I know that God loves me, so what is supposed to be happening here?”
It is precisely because He loves us that we’re having these tempering, refining experiences. God knows, and we are here to learn, that we must become like Him so we can live with Him!
And a godlike life is carved from the very things that make it hard—the gut-wrenching things that happen and the righteous desires that haven’t.
I testify that during those sanctifying experiences, when growth is taking place and God is at work, our stories may not look like success to others. In fact, on the outside it may look like things are sort of unraveling or falling apart, and it will certainly feel that way.
God is shaping us into something only He knows we can become.
Still, like Nephi, I do not know the meaning of all things.
When I spoke at Ryan’s funeral, I looked at his wife, Cari, and their four children with such a heavy heart and said, “I don’t understand why this happened. I don’t. But let me be clear: Not understanding is not the same as not believing.”
I may not understand everything, but I absolutely believe God sees you, loves you, and knows your story—a story that is both personal and purposeful!
Your story is personal. So you don’t need to look sideways and ask, “How come my life doesn’t look like theirs?”
And it’s purposeful in that it has meaning. Our suffering means something. It’s not a detour from the path; it gives purpose to our path.
God is intimately aware of your experience and has a plan for all of it—for each one of us, even if we can’t see it right now.

At Ryan’s funeral, his oldest son, seven-year-old Jaac, shared a Primary talk he and his dad had worked on just two weeks earlier. Jaac said, “I love Lego bricks, and when I get a new box, I open it up and lay out all the pieces and follow the instructions. Just like our Heavenly Father has a plan, and if we follow, it will guide us, and we can build hard things.”
Then Cari asked Jaac, “What would you do if you didn’t have the picture on the box, only the instructions? Would you still stick to the plan?”
He answered, “Yes, because you can trust the one who designed it, and it always turns out.”
But what if you had a beautiful story you thought your life was going to tell, and instead you’ve had to surrender that story? That sting is real, and that wound is wide.
It will take your finest faith in Christ to keep putting together the pieces—the ones that make sense but also the ones that don’t.
Consider this: Christ’s work in your life and His love for you are bigger than your present story. And He can fix what feels badly broken.
The day before Ryan died, he was set apart as the elders quorum president. That afternoon he visited a neighbor whose wife and children had just left him. When Ryan returned, he asked Cari to write down what he had told this man. Ryan said, “Brother, you have a choice right now, and it’s a big one. You can curse God and blame Him, or you can turn to Him and let Him heal you.”
We all have a choice right now. Let’s choose Christ, who can heal the wounds of this world while carving out room for joy!
God is saying, “Trust me,” and we are learning how to say yes.
With an earned conviction, I witness that this—all of this—is the true and only way we can grow and progress and become like our heavenly parents and Savior.
I don’t pretend to know how it works, but it feels like a sort of divine mending that changes what’s happening to you into something happening for you!
Let me leave this last visual image from a sculpting class my brother Kent took in college. He said:
“Our final assignment was to sculpt a bust of ourselves out of clay. I thought to myself, ‘This is going to be easy enough.’
“We began, and I realized it wasn’t easy at all! When I looked at the piece, the eyes were terrible. No matter how hard I tried, I couldn’t get the eyes to look lifelike.
“I observed my classmates and noticed our instructor was helping them. He was very good.
“I, however, didn’t want help. I wanted this to be my piece. I struggled alone for quite a while, until I finally humbled myself and asked for help.
“The instructor came over and deftly started carving; he did it so aggressively and abruptly that it startled me. He dug into the clay much further than I had, and within a few minutes the eyes came to life. It looked so good! There was no way I could have done it.
“As I stepped back and looked at the piece, I could see that it was uniquely me. And yet, without a doubt, a master’s hand had shaped what mine could not.”
My friends, there is sculpting taking place within each of our souls. To invite the Savior to become involved is hard. Our pride gets in the way.
He’ll lovingly chasten us to get our attention, but He waits for an invitation before He can really go to work.
Then He will start carving, sometimes surprising us with how abrupt and aggressive the work feels.
But as time goes on, we will begin to see the work of His hand. God is shaping us into something only He knows we can become.
And one day, when all the suffering and loneliness have ended and our pain is gone, we will be able to step back and look into the mirror of our own soul. Then we will “stand all amazed” and feel to fall at the Savior’s feet and thank Him. We will thank Him for all of it—the molding, the shaping, the pain, and the adversity that have helped us become more like Him.
“For we shall see him as he is,” and “we shall be like him,” I joyfully testify in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Gérald Caussé
title: The Gift of Testimony
content:
Eighteen years ago, Valérie and I received a telephone call from President Thomas S. Monson, during which he called me to serve as a General Authority Seventy. We accepted in faith, knowing that this calling would profoundly change the course of our lives.
The next morning, as I prayed for comfort and guidance, I felt prompted to open a copy of the magazine lying on our kitchen table. Almost immediately, my eyes found this reassuring promise from the Lord: “Be of good cheer, and do not fear, for I the Lord am with you, and will stand by you; and ye shall bear record of me, even Jesus Christ.”
That scripture brought peace to my heart. I realized that my primary responsibility was simply to bear witness of the Savior. Everything else would be in His hands.
Eleven months ago, I was reminded of that same promise under remarkable circumstances. I had just been called to serve as one of the Lord’s Apostles and was invited to join the First Presidency and the Twelve in their sacred meeting room. You can imagine how I felt—astonished, humbled, and deeply moved.
President Dallin H. Oaks invited me to bear my testimony of Jesus Christ. As I prepared to speak, a feeling of peace again filled my heart and those familiar words returned with power: “Be of good cheer, and do not fear, … and ye shall bear record of me, even Jesus Christ.”
In that sacred moment, I knew that nothing could be more meaningful, as my first act as a newly ordained Apostle, than to bear witness of the Redeemer of the world.

Special Witnesses

As recorded in the New Testament, before ascending to His Father, the resurrected Savior gave His Apostles this unequivocal charge: “Ye shall be witnesses unto me.”
Today, in the restored Church of Jesus Christ, the apostolic witness remains central to our doctrine and compelling evidence of its truth. As the Prophet Joseph Smith taught, “The fundamental principles of our religion are the testimony of the Apostles and Prophets, concerning Jesus Christ.”
Each Apostle is called of God and endowed with priesthood keys to be a “special [witness] of the name of Christ in all the world.” Apostles bear a unique, authoritative, divinely empowered witness of the living Christ—of His divine reality, His gospel, His Atonement, and His Resurrection.

Every Member a Witness of Christ

Yet the sacred responsibility to bear witness of Jesus Christ is not limited to prophets and apostles. It extends to all His disciples.
The truth of the restored gospel of Jesus Christ is manifest in the lives of millions of His followers throughout the world. Through your testimonies, in word and deed, you demonstrate the reality of a loving Savior and of the blessings that come through His gospel.
Bearing witness is a foundational responsibility of discipleship. As members of the Church who have covenanted to take upon ourselves the name of Christ, sharing our witness of God and His Son is an essential way to keep that sacred covenant. As taught in the Book of Mormon, covenant disciples will “stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places.”

A Precious Gift from God

The gift of testimony is deeply personal. It is received in the intimacy of our relationship with God and shaped according to our unique experiences, circumstances, and needs. It grows through faith, earnest seeking, gospel living, and the quiet influence of the Holy Ghost. Truly, “to know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God” is one of life’s greatest blessings and a precious gift from God.
Your testimony may be different from mine or that of other family members or fellow Saints. Please trust it, nurture it, and bear it, because it is uniquely yours.

A Gift to Be Shared

Like many of you, I have often wondered, “Why me? Why was I so privileged to receive a testimony of the restored gospel?” I never found a fully satisfying answer. Over time, however, I came to ask a better question: “What does the Lord expect me to do with this gift?”
Our testimony is not a talent to be hidden. It is a gift to be shared—with grateful hearts and in a spirit of humility and love.

Expressing Love Through Testifying

Testimony and love are deeply connected gifts that echo and strengthen one another.
To say “I know” is a tender expression of love toward our neighbor. Because we love others, we naturally desire to share with them the most precious gift we have received—our witness of Jesus Christ and His gospel.
In turn, saying “I love you” with a pure and sincere heart is a way of bearing testimony of Jesus Christ. Whenever we express Christlike love to those around us, we bear witness of Him, the source of all perfect love.
Brothers and sisters, I hope you will fill your lives, and the lives of others, with many heartfelt I knows—as I hope you already do with many I love yous. As these expressions of faith and love come together, they will help create an environment where the Spirit of the Lord can dwell and bring joy to your hearts.

We Can All Testify

One of our nieces recently shared an experience from her youth. She said: “A few years ago, when I was beginning to gain a testimony, I bore my testimony at a Young Women camp. I was so nervous that I only managed to say two simple sentences: ‘I know that God loves me’ and ‘I know that God has a plan for me.’ In the days that followed, I felt discouraged because I wished I could speak like the other girls. I talked with my mom, and she asked, ‘Do you believe what you said?’ ‘Yes,’ I replied. ‘Then that’s all that matters,’ she said.”
Her mother was right. There is great power in a sincere, humble, and heartfelt testimony. It need not be long, eloquent, or dramatic—it only needs to be true.
Each of us can bear such a witness, for it is the Spirit—not words—that testifies of the truth. As the Lord promised, when one speaks by the power of the Holy Ghost, “the Holy Ghost shall be shed forth in bearing record unto all things whatsoever ye shall say.”
Throughout history, countless seekers of truth have been transformed by the testimonies of humble servants of the Lord—those whom He calls “the weak and the simple.”
From Enoch and Moses to Joseph Smith, and to the more than 90,000 missionaries serving throughout the world today, the pattern is the same. They stand and declare what they know to be true. Their words may be simple and their speech imperfect, but their witness carries divine power because it is confirmed by the Holy Ghost.

Changing Lives Through Testifying

Brothers and sisters, do you realize that your testimony can literally change lives—your own and the lives of others?
As you share it freely, your own testimony will grow stronger. You will draw closer to the Lord and feel more deeply the power of His redemption. In turn, you will become instruments in His hands to bless and minister to those around you.
At a moment of deep anguish, the young Alma remembered having “heard [his] father prophesy … concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ … to atone for the sins of the world.” That remembered witness from his father became the spark of hope that led him to repent and completely change his life.
How many “Almas” are there around you waiting to hear your witness and discover, or rediscover, the hope that is found in Jesus Christ?

Seeking Opportunities to Testify

If you have received the gift of a testimony—even if it is only the beginning of one—it is your duty and privilege to share it.
I invite you to look each day for opportunities, as prompted by the Holy Ghost, to bear witness of Jesus Christ and His restored gospel—even if only for a minute or two. A brief and sincere expression of faith can make a profound difference—whether at home with your family, in testimony meetings, in ministering visits and missionary lessons, on social media, or in simple, everyday interactions with others. You can share your beliefs in simple and natural ways, such as “I love our Savior, Jesus Christ” or “The gospel brings joy to my heart.”
Imagine what could happen if all of us—millions of disciples of Jesus Christ—consistently shared our testimonies. Countless lives would be blessed, faith would grow, and the love of Christ would spread more abundantly throughout the world.

My Testimony

As a servant of the Lord and one of His special witnesses, I am profoundly grateful for the gift of testimony I have received through the power of God. I solemnly declare that we have a loving Heavenly Father and that His Son, Jesus Christ, is the Savior of the world and the source of “every good gift.” I express my earnest desire to serve Them and to bear witness of Them continually, all the days of my life. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Vaiangina Sikahema
title: Prophets, Seers, and Revelators
content:
In 1947, my maternal grandparents, Sione Tufui and Salote Tongi Wolfgramm, were serving a full-time mission in Niuatoputapu, a small, isolated volcanic island in the Kingdom of Tonga in the South Pacific. My grandparents were poor farmers with no formal education. Grampa was 28, Gramma was 25, and with them were their three children: my mother, Potenitila (Ruby), age 4; Makeleta (Maggie), age 3; and 9-month-old Vilimanulea, at the time their only son.
With limited visas for Americans, Tongan couples like the Wolfgramms were routinely called to serve on neighboring islands or in villages as “senior” couple missionaries.

In June of that same year, Apostle Matthew Cowley, who was over the Pacific, was coming to Tonga. Only twice before had an Apostle visited our island kingdom: David O. McKay in 1921, followed by George Albert Smith in 1938.
For Saints scattered across the Pacific, having an Apostle of the Lord among them was the chance of a lifetime. Reaching the Apostle meant a long voyage for my grandparents across the largest body of water on the planet to the main island of Tongatapu, but first stopping midway on their home island of Vava‘u. The Pacific is known for its fickle weather patterns, and the week of their trip was no different.

The Wolfgramms sailed into a storm; a journey that should have taken 16 hours to Vava‘u stretched into two and a half brutal days at sea. From my Gramma’s journal, she wrote: “We were completely soaked, … battered, and sick, … too weak to eat. … I held Vilimanulea to my chest until finally arriving to Vava‘u.”
Yet their trial was not over. The storm left the baby severely dehydrated. With no medicine, the Wolfgramms’ precious son died of exposure. Within two days, they buried their baby in Vava‘u and continued their voyage.
For the Wolfgramms, burying their infant child was akin to the pioneers who buried their children on the trail to Zion. Like the early pioneers, they yearned to hear and be in the presence of an Apostle.
Grieving with empty arms, my grandparents got back on the boat, their mission not yet complete.
They were sailing toward an Apostle, who held priesthood keys, held the authority for the ordinances that would later seal them as an eternal family. They sailed to sit at the feet of an Apostle, who would teach them their duty so they could bless others on their island with the message of the restored gospel of Jesus Christ.
You see, my grandparents understood that the gospel restored by Joseph Smith revealed truths previously withheld from them. Joseph helped restore the Savior’s Church with prophets, seers, and revelators who held priesthood keys that would one day bind them together as a family forever.
My grandparents girded up their loins, fresh courage took (see “Come, Come, Ye Saints,”, no. 30), and sailed to be with Elder Matthew Cowley.
For centuries after the deaths of the ancient apostles and prophets until the boy Joseph knelt in the grove of trees near Palmyra, New York, there was no revelation to prophets. An Old Testament prophet called it a famine:
“Behold, the days come … that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord:
“And [people] shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the Lord, and shall not find it” (Amos 8:11–12).
That same Old Testament prophet, Amos, also declared, “Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7).
The Savior foretold of false prophets who would decimate His ancient Church (see Matthew 7:15–23). The Apostle Paul also taught, “For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock” (Acts 20:29).
Reformers in the Middle Ages sought and yearned for prophetic voices but could not find them.
Even in modern times, there are people who thirst to hear prophetic direction and guidance.
The Lord gave Joseph Smith this counsel: “And all they who receive the oracles of God, let them beware how they hold them lest they are accounted as a light thing” (Doctrine and Covenants 90:5).
I suspect the Lord knew that even when we would have these devices (cell phones) to easily see and hear His anointed servants, many of us would still take them for granted.
In a general conference address over 20 years ago, President Jeffrey R. Holland asked: “Are the heavens open? Does God reveal His will to prophets and apostles as in days of old? That they are and that He does is the unflinching declaration of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to all the world. And in that declaration lies the significance of Joseph Smith, the Prophet, for nearly 200 years now” (“Prophets, Seers, and Revelators,”, Nov. 2004, 8).
Joseph described the moment the heavens opened this way: “When the light rested upon me I saw two Personages, whose brightness and glory defy all description, standing above me in the air. One of them spake unto me, calling me by name and said, pointing to the other—This is My Beloved Son. Hear Him!” (Joseph Smith—History 1:17).
With that clear, simple, and understated introduction, the Father and His Son, Jesus Christ, would begin the work of restoring the Savior’s ancient Church through a then-teenage boy in upstate New York.
In the years that followed this momentous event, greater truths, priesthood authority, sacred ordinances, additional scriptures, and knowledge of God’s plan of salvation would all be restored or rediscovered through the Prophet Joseph Smith.
Perhaps you can appreciate why my beloved grandparents were so eager to be in the presence of one of the Lord’s anointed. Even in their despair and while mourning the tragic loss of their only son—their handsome, cheerful little boy—they solemnly buried him and made the Herculean effort to sail just to listen to an Apostle of the Lord.
What a blessing it is to live in a time when apostles and prophets are on the earth. As we begin this opening session of the 196th Semiannual General Conference of the Church, let us not be guilty of holding “the oracles of God … as a light thing” (Doctrine and Covenants 90:5).
It is interesting to note that when the Church was only about one and a half years old, some early Church leaders opposed the idea of publishing the Lord’s revelations through the Prophet Joseph that would eventually become the Doctrine and Covenants. Some of them were embarrassed by the young prophet’s poor writing skills.
Maybe that’s why the Savior declared, “What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same” (Doctrine and Covenants 1:38; emphasis added).
How grateful I am for noble progenitors who left me and my posterity a legacy of faith and courage in the face of difficulties and obstacles.
I witness of the truths of the restored gospel and of living prophets, seers, and revelators in the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Kevin J. Hathaway
title: Jesus Christ Is the Great Deliverer!
content:
Jesus Christ is the Great Deliverer!
Have you ever felt left out, wondered if you were enough, lost someone you loved, faced illness, experienced family difficulties, or carried a burden no one else could see? My message today is that Jesus Christ delivers the righteous from these and every other affliction of mortality.
Jesus Christ descended below all things and suffered “pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind”; therefore, He comprehends our suffering, is filled with mercy, and knows how to succor us according to our infirmities. With perfect understanding and infinite power, He can deliver the righteous from all things, forever. His deliverance is certain; the question for most righteous followers is not if He will deliver but how and when He will do so.
Our family experienced a sudden trial and the Lord’s deliverance as we drove in two cars to begin our service as mission leaders. While driving in a construction zone, two large tires came loose from a semitruck and struck both cars at high speed. The airbags deployed, the cars were destroyed, and we were left stranded on the roadside wondering why this had happened when we had left everything to serve the Lord.
In that moment, the Spirit brought us peace: Everything would be all right. We were not immediately delivered from the trial, but that assurance gave us hope in the deliverance that would come. With the help of many wonderful people, we arrived on time and began our mission without serious injury.
The experience on that freeway illustrates a scriptural pattern of divine deliverance as follows: Opposition brings heartrending questions and emotions, sincere seeking invites assurances, Christ’s grace enables us to endure and grow, and deliverance comes in the Savior’s time and way.
Let us consider each part of the pattern.

Opposition, Heartrending Questions, and Emotions

Opposition comes to all, even the righteous. It can stir heartrending questions and deep emotions, like Joseph Smith’s cry from Liberty Jail, “O God, where art thou?” or the grief and fear felt by Helaman’s stripling warriors. Such questions and emotions are not sin or weakness; they can create a sacred space where agency is activated and we choose whether to turn toward Jesus Christ.

Sincere Spiritual Seeking

Sincere seeking means turning toward Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ through heartfelt prayer, purposeful fasting, and scripture study. Alma’s people in bondage “began to cry mightily to God.” King Darius fasted through the night as he waited for Daniel’s deliverance from the lions’ den. Such acts of faith draw us closer to Jesus Christ.

Assurances of Deliverance

As we humbly and patiently keep our covenants, the Savior will visit us in our afflictions and bring assurances of deliverance. Many in the scriptures received assurances of peace, faith, and hope for deliverance in Christ.
Sister Kenzie Brinkerhoff was visited in her afflictions and given sacred assurances as well. On the last preparation day before Sister Brinkerhoff returned home from her mission, her father, Kelly, called early in the morning to tell her he loved her, was proud of her, and was excited to hug her soon. Heartbreakingly, while driving home from work that night, Kelly was in a vehicle accident and passed away. When my wife and I arrived soon after Kenzie received the news, she was grieving deeply. Through her tears came the heartrending question, “President, how could this happen when I was one week away from hugging my dad?”
Several weeks later I called to ask how she was dealing with her father’s passing, and she said: “The past few weeks have been the most awful and the most sacred time in my life. I have never clung so tightly to my covenants. I know that Jesus knows what this feels like, and He will heal me.”

Enabled Enduring Through the Grace of Jesus Christ

Enabled enduring comes through the grace of Jesus Christ and strengthens us to “cheerfully do all things that lie in our power” and then “stand still, with the utmost assurance, to see the salvation of God, and for his arm to be revealed.” This grace does not remove the pain and difficulty of affliction; it is an enabling power that allows us, after all we can do, to receive divine strength beyond our own and lay hold on eternal promises through Jesus Christ.
As Kenzie binds herself to Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ in prayer, obedience, and covenant keeping, They help her endure what she cannot bear alone. That same enabling grace is available to all who turn to Jesus Christ.

Divine Deliverance According to His Time and His Way

As we wait upon the Lord and exercise faith in Him, needed growth and spiritual stretching come, and the Savior delivers us from our afflictions and consecrates them for our gain. He does this in His time and way.
To Kenzie and all who wait for divine deliverance, I testify that the Lord is not delayed, distracted, or derelict in His deliverance. He has not forgotten you. He does not take joy in your suffering. However, He knows that lessons learned while waiting can bring converting growth that an earlier rescue might not produce.
But what of moments when the hour seems too late, the loss too final, and deliverance appears impossible? Surely, Jairus must have felt the time had passed and deliverance was impossible when he received news that his daughter had died. But Jesus said, “Be not afraid, only believe.” Holding on to that assurance, Jairus watched the Savior deliver his daughter from death, showing that no mortal timeline can place us beyond Christ’s power to deliver.
When deliverance feels impossible, remember Elder Patrick Kearon’s witness: “Jesus specializes in the seemingly impossible. He came here to make the impossible possible, the irredeemable redeemable, to heal the unhealable, to right the unrightable, to promise the unpromisable. And He’s really good at it. In fact, He’s perfect at it.”
To all who continue to face the pain, fear, and loneliness of life, I echo the Savior’s words: “Be not afraid, only believe.” In His time and way, Jesus Christ will deliver you. Some miracles are immediate, some come after long waiting, and some await the Resurrection.
May we hear, believe, and act on our “great Deliv’rer’s” reassuring voice when He says, “I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick.” I testify that Jesus Christ is the Great Deliverer, now and forever, in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Ulisses Soares
title: A Higher and Holier Fast
content:
My beloved brothers and sisters, I have prayerfully pondered the sacred blessings our Heavenly Father and His Beloved Son, Jesus Christ, offer us as we draw near to Them through sincere and faithful observance of the law of the fast. Therefore, this morning, from the bottom of my heart, I testify of the sanctifying spiritual power that flows into our lives as we seek to live this law in a higher and holier way. This divine pattern of devotion brings strength, guidance, peace, and divine help to sustain us throughout our mortal journey.
The Lord’s call to fast in these latter days is an echo of the message He gave through the Old Testament prophet Isaiah—a message of healing, covenant power, and divine blessing that continues to be offered to all of God’s children. In Isaiah chapter 58, the Lord lifted the vision of His covenant people beyond the outward observance of this law. He also revealed its divine purpose as an act of worship that shapes and refines our discipleship and draws us closer to Him.
Isaiah beautifully recorded the blessings promised to those who faithfully live this law:
“Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily. …
“Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am.”
What a tender promise: light after darkness, healing after weariness, and the comforting assurance that when we call upon the Lord, He is near. President Joseph F. Smith taught that proper fasting “would … place the body in subjection to the spirit, and so promote communion with the Holy Ghost” and that “this law would bring [us] nearer to God.”
A sincere and faithful fast is accompanied by earnest and intentional prayer. As we lift our hearts to the Lord in humility, fasting becomes an expression of our desire to draw near to Him, communicate the true desires of our hearts, and understand His will for us. Through the union of fasting and prayer, our faith, love, and devotion to Him deepen. We become more humble and more aware of our complete dependence upon the Lord. Our hearts are softened, our souls become more receptive to the influence of the Holy Ghost, and we are better prepared to receive personal revelation and move forward along the covenant path.
This divine pattern finds its highest and holiest expression in the life of Jesus Christ. As in all things, the Savior did not merely teach divine principles—He exemplified them perfectly. Before His earthly ministry began, He withdrew into the wilderness and spent 40 days communing with His Father. He was the Only Begotten Son of God in the flesh, and of all the things He could have done to prepare for His sacred mission, He chose to seek complete alignment with His Father’s will through earnest fasting and prayer. Spiritually fortified, the Savior triumphed over the temptations of the adversary, began His mortal ministry, and fulfilled His divine destiny as Redeemer of the world. His example teaches us that fasting and prayer may not remove every burden from our path, but they draw heaven near and endow us with divine power to overcome or endure whatever circumstances we may face, giving us the spiritual fortitude to remain faithful to the Father’s will.
Adopting this holy pattern of fasting is more than a physical test of restraint or a petition for specific blessings. It is an elevating expression of faith and trust in the Lord through which our hearts can be filled with rejoicing as we commune with Him more deeply. It is a way to align our desires with His purposes, and our expectations with His wisdom. Even when answers do not come in the way we expect, fasting and prayer help us develop greater confidence in the Lord, in our covenants with Him, and in His plan for our lives, as well as a deeper willingness to accept His will.
Through this holy law, the Lord also invites us to look beyond ourselves and turn our hearts toward His children. Isaiah taught that an acceptable fast helps us “to let the oppressed go free” and to “break every yoke.” The Prophet Joseph Smith once taught, “A man filled with the love of God, is not content with blessing his family alone, but ranges through the whole world, anxious to bless the whole human race.” Thus, our fast becomes not only a personal act of devotion to God but also an outward expression of Christlike charity and love.
In our day, our desire to help “the oppressed go free” and “break every yoke,” as the Lord taught through the prophet Isaiah, finds tangible expression in generous fast offerings. Each contribution reflects a willing heart, faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, and a sincere desire to bless those in need. This spirit of generosity also reflects the Savior’s own example. He came down from heaven, dwelt among the children of men, and suffered “pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind … that he [might] know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.” As we follow His perfect example by seeking to succor God’s children, our hearts are opened to the needs of others, and we become better prepared to minister in a more Christlike way.
Though our fast offerings may seem small and simple, they become consecrated expressions of compassion, concern, and service. As we give generously—not only for the benefit of those in need but also as an expression of our love for the Lord and our commitment to His work—we consecrate both our means and our time to Him. In doing so, we give more fully of ourselves to the building of the kingdom of God. As we embrace this spirit of consecration, the Lord guides and strengthens us to become instruments in His hands.
I have personally witnessed how the blessings of fasting often enter people’s lives quietly and tenderly—softening hearts, strengthening testimonies, sanctifying souls, and transforming lives. I have also seen sacred blessings come to those who turn their hearts toward God’s children through generous fast offerings. Personally, I have felt an increase of inspiration and revelation as I have sought to live this law with greater sincerity. Fasting, when observed with joy and joined with prayer and generosity, brings sweeter communion with the Lord and a deeper, more personal connection with Him.
My dear friends, I invite you to prayerfully ponder Isaiah’s teachings and more intentionally embrace the divine purpose of the law of the fast in a higher and holier way as part of our worship. As you do so, I promise, in the name of our Savior, Jesus Christ, that miracles will come into your life. You will draw nearer to the Savior, receive strength to overcome your weaknesses, and become more sensitive to the needs of others. Through this divinely appointed practice, the Lord will sanctify us and pour His Spirit and blessings more abundantly into our lives.
I bear my solemn testimony that as we remember, restore, and more fully honor the sacred purpose of the law of the fast with sincere hearts, the Lord will fulfill the promises declared by Isaiah: our “light [shall] break forth as the morning”; our “health shall spring forth speedily”; then shall we “call, and the Lord shall answer”; we shall cry, and He shall say, “Here I am.” Of these things I bear my witness in His holy name, even Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Sean Douglas
title: The Hour of Your Mission Is Come
content:
As a member of the Presiding Bishopric, I have the privilege of serving on the Church’s Missionary Executive Council. I have a deep love for the missionaries of the Church. They are uniquely set apart from the world and divinely commissioned by the Savior. As President Dallin H. Oaks teaches: “We invite all [of God’s children] to come unto Christ by repentance and baptism and confirmation in order to open the doors of the celestial kingdom to the sons and daughters of God. No one else can do this.” Missionaries are called to assist in this great work.
Today more missionaries are serving in more missions and more of God’s children are choosing to enter the Lord’s Church through baptism than ever before in this dispensation.
We love missionaries of all ages. You are an army of righteousness with the doctrine of Christ as your purpose. You are a force of faith, power, love, and joy. You are what you preach. You are not only the messengers but also living examples of the message. Make no mistake—you are doing the most important work you could be doing. We thank you for building up the kingdom of God on earth.
A few months ago, I attended a sacrament meeting where my two great-nephews, who are brothers, spoke before departing for their missions. They were beaming with enthusiasm and eager to get going. Maybe it was because their assignments are thousands of miles from home at opposite ends of the earth. But in truth, their desire to serve the Lord was unmistakable.
They reminded me of the sons of Mosiah in the Book of Mormon, who “were desirous that salvation should be declared to every creature, for they could not bear that any human soul should perish.”
Their desire to serve the Lord rose above every other personal ambition. It’s what makes missionaries special; it’s why they radiate the Light of Christ and teach with convincing power. For a season, all else takes a back seat—education, dating, careers, family time, and even sleeping in on Saturday mornings. Yes, the Lord’s expectations are high for you! But, oh, is it worth it! President Russell M. Nelson taught, “Nothing else compares in magnitude, nothing else compares in importance, nothing else compares in majesty.”
God held you in reserve for this time. You were taught and prepared, before you were born, to invite God’s children to come unto Christ. We could say this is in your spiritual DNA. Take care not to become distracted. Prioritize it; don’t let anything get in the way. You are needed!
Sister Douglas and I served as mission leaders in Lima, Peru. One of our amazing missionaries was Elder Merlin Sanchez. Merlin was baptized when he was nearly 24 years old. As some do, he stopped participating for a time. A faithful friend helped him begin to fill out his mission papers and schedule a physical exam, even though Merlin had not yet decided to serve a mission.

With the help of friends and leaders, Merlin returned to church at age 25. A desire to serve a mission suddenly swelled in his heart. Thankfully, his mission papers were well advanced. Once he made the decision to go, it was miraculous to see how the Lord removed seemingly insurmountable obstacles one by one. When I asked him why he wanted to serve, he replied, “I only want to be close to Jesus Christ and to follow Him.”

He became a wonderful missionary, converted to Jesus Christ and His doctrine. His every experience, trial, and companion was consecrated for his gain. Interestingly, Elder Sanchez served with the same companion twice, for a total of eight months. Though opposite in personality, they became united in purpose—assigned together by divine design.
Merlin met his eternal sweetheart, Gali, just a few months following his mission. On the day of their marriage, he was called to be a bishop—quite the wedding gift! There was no time for his discipleship to be interrupted or his faith to be diminished. After all, serving a mission is just one of many significant steps on the path of lifelong discipleship.

Merlin and Gali today have a beautiful family with three children, while Merlin serves as a stake president. They cannot fathom what their lives would be if Merlin had not served a mission.
To you wonderful young converts of the Church, a mission may not have been on your radar, but it ought to be now. To all the rising generation of the Church, I invite you to place serving a full-time mission high on your list. Don’t be distracted by alternatives of far less worth. Some might be like Amulek of the Book of Mormon, who expressed, “For I was called many times and I would not hear.”
Prophets of God today strongly reaffirm “that the Lord has asked every worthy, able young man to prepare for and serve a mission. For [you], missionary service is a priesthood responsibility. … For you young and able sisters, a mission is also a powerful, but optional, opportunity. … Pray to know if the Lord would have you serve a mission.”
We rejoice exceedingly for your faithful response to the prophet’s call to action. Record numbers of missionaries of all ages are finding great joy as they humbly dedicate themselves to serving the Lord by laboring among Heavenly Father’s children. I wish to wholeheartedly add: There is still plenty of room and a special place reserved for each one of you! We need you! “Come join the ranks!”
You have a testimony of Jesus Christ and His Atonement that can bless a world suffering without knowledge of His divine mission. I pray that you will make the Savior’s grand commission your very own.
I conclude with the words of our Savior given through Joseph Smith to Thomas B. Marsh, who was called to preach the gospel in 1830. I invite each of you to substitute your name for Thomas’s:
“Thomas, my son [or daughter], …
“Lift up your heart and rejoice, for the hour of your mission is come; and your tongue shall be loosed, and you shall declare glad tidings of great joy unto this generation. …
“Therefore, thrust in your sickle with all your soul, and your sins are forgiven you, and you shall be laden with sheaves upon your back. … Wherefore, your family shall live.
“Behold, … go from them only for a little time, and declare my word, and I will prepare a place for them.
“… I will open the hearts of the people, and they will receive you. And I will establish a church by your hand.”
In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: D. Todd Christofferson
title: O Be Wise
content:
Today I feel a bit like the Book of Mormon prophet Jacob, when he felt compelled by the Spirit to address subjects that were not particularly edifying, having to use “boldness of speech,” as he put it, instead of feasting on “the pleasing word of God.” So, with a sense of duty, I turn to the subject of gambling.
President Gordon B. Hinckley, in addressing this subject over 20 years ago, mentioned a story about former United States President Calvin Coolidge, known as a man of few words. As Coolidge returned home from church one Sunday, his wife asked him what the preacher spoke about. He replied, “Sin.”
“Well, what did he say?” she asked.
“He was against it,” replied Coolidge.
President Hinckley said, “I think I could answer the question concerning gambling just that briefly. We are against it.”
Putting money or something of value at risk to bet on a particular outcome or event is an activity that has plagued mankind almost, I suppose, from the beginning of time. And time has not made it any more worthwhile or any less harmful. Unfortunately, in recent years, gambling has become incredibly pervasive.
The smartphone has transformed gambling from an occasional activity requiring a trip to a casino, racetrack, or lottery kiosk into an activity available continuously, privately, and almost anywhere. This has led to an explosion in gambling. Worldwide surveys spanning multiple years indicate that 46 percent of adults gambled in the last 12 months—that is about 2.3 billion people. The global gambling industry generated estimated revenues of $758 billion in 2025. Of course, the industry’s revenue is the gambler’s loss. Simply put, the industry’s entire business model is built on its customers losing money.
The growth in worldwide gambling is primarily driven by three new online markets. First is online sports betting, which involves wagers on sports scores, statistics, or events. Second is online casino-type games, sometimes referred to as internet or iGaming: slot games, roulette, blackjack, poker, and so on. A third, relatively new platform is what are called “prediction markets” that allow participants to bet on whether something will or will not happen and when. It could be tied to anything: interest rates, elections, sports, wildfires, or even, if you can imagine, the timing of the Second Coming.
Youth and young adults are disproportionately affected. For this demographic, impulsivity and peer influence are compounded by early exposure, easy online access, and intense marketing. Widespread social acceptance only adds to the enticement. Sports betting is especially rampant among teenagers and young adults. It easily becomes consuming and often compulsive. It robs time from studies, relationships, and career development. It crowds out things of value and in their place fosters greed.
In the United States, 36 percent of boys age 11 to 17 reported gambling last year, rising from 32 percent at age 11 to 49 percent—virtually half of all boys—at age 17. Equally troubling is the substantial percentage of 18- to 29-year-old women who now participate in gambling each year, especially mobile sports betting, slots, and lotteries.
Surveys reveal that people know that in gambling the odds are stacked against them, and the house always wins—they just don’t think it will win against them personally. But the central risk of gambling is not merely that customers lose money on individual wagers. The larger concern is that continuous, mobile access can transform occasional entertainment into repeated behavior that displaces saving, increases debt, and creates far-reaching family and social costs. I have to agree with George Washington when he said of gambling, “It is the child of avarice—the brother of inequity—and father of mischief” (although calling it “mischief” may be too mild).
Earlier this year a prominent journalist wrote in magazine about his preplanned, monthslong experience with sports gambling. Among other things, he noted: “Experts estimate that only about 2 to 5 percent of gamblers will develop compulsive behaviors. But … that small percentage becomes a very large number when tens of millions of [people] suddenly have casinos in their pockets.”
He concluded: “As a society, we are making an enormously risky bet: that we can reap the rewards of a runaway gambling industry without paying any price; [we are betting] that the litany of social ills long associated with this vice—addiction and impoverishment, isolation and abuse, cheating and … corrosive idleness—can, this time, be kept in check; [we are betting] that, unlike every civilization that came before us, we can beat the house.”
At different times, President Dallin H. Oaks has reminded us that “as we make current decisions, we should always be asking, ‘Where will this lead?’ … What is the effect on our future of the decisions we make in the present?” President Oaks points out that each choice has an “opportunity cost,” that is, “if we spend time doing one thing, we lose the opportunity to do another.” What is the opportunity cost of gambling? What do you forgo in terms of money, time, relationships, and worthwhile pursuits? Where does it lead?
Perhaps you think your character and your commitment to divine covenants are sufficiently strong that, for you, wagers would never become more than occasional, casual fun. Maybe. But whether you are right about that or not, have you considered how your example might affect others?
If your moral standing is secure, then undoubtedly there are others who look to you as a guide for upright living. That would certainly be true for your children but also others that you may or may not know who are watching and learning from what they see in you. They may be newer or weaker in the faith. A little gambling that seemingly has only a minor impact in your life may be more costly to them if they take license from your example.
The Apostle Paul noted in his day that someone with a firm belief in Christ could eat food sacrificed to idols without intending it as a sign of idol worship; it would just be a meal. But he cautioned the disciples to abstain anyway.
“Take heed,” he said, “lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
“For if any man see thee which hast knowledge [of the gospel] sit at meat in the idol’s temple, shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened to eat those things which are offered to idols;
“And through thy [conduct] shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?”
In the context of my message today, Paul is saying, “Since your recreational gambling may lead a weaker brother or sister into temptation, just don’t do it. Every soul is precious, and Christ died for him, for her, as He did for you.”
For us as Latter-day Saints, overarching all other concerns is the fact that gambling is morally wrong. Gambling is built on the desire to obtain something for nothing. Its structure requires that any gain comes at others’ expense. It’s hard to reconcile that with the commandment to love our neighbor as ourselves. In addition, our resources are stewardships, and the question is not merely whether a purchase is legal but whether it builds anything—in us, in our families, or in those around us. In the end, gambling produces nothing of value and enriches only its purveyors.
President Oaks clearly stated the moral case against gambling some years ago in these words: “What does gambling do to its participants? The attitude of taking something from someone else in order to enhance our own position—[which is] the essence of gambling—leads us away from the giving path of Christ and toward the taking path of the adversary. The act of taking or trying to take something from someone else without giving value in return is destructive of spiritual sensitivities.”
Today, I am pleading with all of us to live life on a higher plane. God has granted life and agency to each of us, and each of us is accountable to Him for how we live that life. A key part of a life well-lived is contributing to the well-being of others. It is being productive in worthy endeavors. It is being and doing better without others doing worse. It comes by supporting and rewarding work rather than idle pursuits. Work leads to prosperous, just, and equitable societies. Gambling, even for fun, leads in the opposite direction.
Remembering President Oaks’s comments about “opportunity cost” and the opportunities lost when a person devotes time and money to gambling, my plea again is not only to refrain from gambling but to use the time and resources saved thereby for doing good. The Lord counsels us to “be anxiously engaged in a good cause, … and bring to pass much righteousness.” Indeed, “blessed are all they who do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled with the Holy Ghost.” If we hunger and thirst after righteousness, there are many good things we will pursue and other things that, because they are incompatible with righteousness, we will put out of our lives entirely.
I pray that you will not treat gambling lightly. Having begun these remarks quoting the prophet Jacob, I end with another of his statements: “O be wise; what can I say more?” In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Dale G. Renlund
title: “How Long Will It Be Ere They Believe Me?”
content:
In the late 1980s, Mr. Martin developed severe heart failure. Despite the most advanced medications available, his heart could not adequately support his circulation. He would die without a heart transplant. He became my team’s patient, and the wait for a donor heart began. His condition worsened, and mechanical pumps were implanted to sustain his life.
A few days later, Mr. Martin’s liver, kidneys, and lungs began to fail. If a donor heart did not become available soon, he would surely die. One became available, and Mr. Martin received a transplant. Surprisingly, this new heart did not work well, and his condition was now even worse. After a couple of days, the situation seemed hopeless, and we were preparing to withdraw life support. While discussing the limited options with Mrs. Martin, I was notified that another donor heart was available. This donor heart was considered marginal and would not be used for any other recipient in the country. With Mrs. Martin’s consent, we decided to use this marginal heart for a second transplant.
Fortunately, the marginal heart functioned beautifully. Within hours, Mr. Martin’s liver, kidneys, and lungs began to recover, and the mechanical pumps were removed. Ten days later, I walked into Mr. Martin’s hospital room, knowing that he would be discharged from the hospital the next day. He was sitting on his bed, gripping his breakfast tray, and was clearly irritated. I asked what was wrong. Through clenched teeth, Mr. Martin replied, “The oatmeal isn’t hot, and the milk isn’t cold!”
For the past three weeks, Mr. Martin had hovered near death yet was now complaining about the hospital food! (I think when you go through something like Mr. Martin did, you use up all your coping coupons. And I don’t think anybody should be tortured with oatmeal regardless of temperature.) But at that moment, Mr. Martin focused on the cold oatmeal in front of him and seemingly dismissed the miracle he had experienced. He lost sight of the bigger picture, both where he had been and the promise the future now held.
We too can easily fall into the same trap that Mr. Martin did that morning in the hospital, especially when our day-to-day challenges loom. We focus on the here and now—the “cold oatmeal”—and lose sight of the bigger picture, both where we have been and God’s promises to us.
This is not just a modern phenomenon. As recorded in the Old Testament, the Lord led the children of Israel out of slavery in Egypt. God saved them when they were trapped at the Red Sea and provided for them when they lacked food and water. Even when they complained about a monotonous diet, the Lord miraculously helped them. They survived because of God’s miracles, yet they repeatedly focused on cold oatmeal. As they overlooked both the Lord’s blessings and His promises, their trust eroded in God and in God’s prophet, Moses.
When the children of Israel reached the promised land, they were intimidated by the challenges ahead. They again bemoaned their situation, saying, “Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt! or would God we had died in this wilderness!” In other words, they thought that they had it better before and that this challenge was surely too much, even for the Lord.
Scripture records the Lord’s response: “And the Lord said unto Moses, … how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have [shown] among them?” In other words, the Lord was asking: “Why don’t they trust me? Despite all I have done, why won’t they believe me?” How often the Lord reassured the children of Israel, and reassures us, of His constancy, declaring, “I will never break my covenant with you.”
Perhaps you have been served more than your share of cold oatmeal. Perhaps, like the children of Israel, you have doubted God’s care for you, His willingness to succor you, or His capacity to keep His promises. Yet God invites us to trust Him and His promises.
During His mortal ministry, the Savior told His disciples: “These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” Jesus overcame the world; we do not have to do so ourselves. When our faith is centered on Jesus Christ, He promises spiritual peace no matter our circumstances. We can experience joy in our here and now because of Him and through our covenant relationship with Him.
Faith in Jesus Christ frees us from uncertainty because our hope rests on His faithfulness and righteousness, not on our own. The prophet Lehi testified to his son Jacob, “Wherefore, I know that thou art redeemed, because of the righteousness of thy Redeemer.” Jacob was a good and faithful person. Yet his righteousness would not be the source of his redemption. No, Jacob’s redemption would come through the righteousness of Jesus Christ. The same is true for each of us.
One of the purposes of the Book of Mormon is to show us “what great things the Lord hath done … that [we] may know the covenants of the Lord, that [we] are not cast off forever.” Moroni exhorts us “that [we should] remember how merciful the Lord hath been unto the children of men [throughout the ages], and ponder it in [our] hearts.”
As we reflect on the great things the Lord has already done and remember His goodness and mercy, we are better positioned to grasp the bigger picture and to rely on His promises to us. We can trust Him.
I remember learning a lesson, one of many, from my younger sister, Linda. She said that she would read her scriptures and see remarkable blessings promised by the Lord. In her mind, though, she saw a big asterisk that seemed to say, “Those blessings apply to everyone—except Linda.” Over the years, Linda came to a different realization. She said, “I am not extraordinary enough to warrant an exception. The blessings are promised to me too.” Linda is extraordinary but still no exception. Neither are you, brothers and sisters; there is no asterisk excluding you from God’s richest blessings. If you think there is, take out a big eraser and obliterate that asterisk. You can rely on God’s promises.
The Prophet Joseph Smith taught that Jesus Christ “knows the situation of both the living and the dead, and has made ample provision for their redemption, according to their several circumstances, and the laws of the kingdom of God, whether in this world, or in the world to come.”
“Ample provision” means that all human circumstances are within the Savior’s redemptive reach. The Atonement of Jesus Christ permitted our Heavenly Father to give the Savior all power “in heaven and in earth.” The power of the Messiah to save and exalt is profoundly intimate and infinite beyond human comprehension; there is more than enough to cover any breach, need, or deficit for all of us, for each of us.
When I consider what Jesus Christ has done for us, I do not think we want Him asking us, “How long will it be ere [you] believe me?” Strive to remember all the times He has inclined His ear to you, especially when confronted with cold oatmeal. With Moroni, I declare, “The eternal purposes of the Lord shall roll on, until all his promises shall be fulfilled.” We can trust the Lord, especially His promises. These promises apply to you. We can joyfully sing:

Standing on the promises of Christ, my King, …
Standing on the promises that cannot fail …
Standing on the promises, I cannot fall, …
Standing on the promises of God.

I know that God lives and that Jesus is the Christ. Not only that, but I also know that Their “exceeding great and precious promises” are sure and “that by these [we] might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world.” Of this I bear solemn witness in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Timothy L. Farnes
title: Divine Appointments
content:
It’s What We Do, Isn’t It?

I’ll never forget a Saturday almost 20 years ago. I had just been called into a stake presidency and hadn’t yet been released as bishop. We had five young children, a business to run, and a full day of Church meetings, starting at 8:00 a.m. and concluding with a ward temple night. It was a busy time, and I wanted to give my all to the Lord, but I was never sure if I had enough to give.
At a midday leadership meeting, the presiding authority invited questions. I gathered my courage and asked a question about an administrative matter that was troubling me. Instead of getting a helpful answer, I felt like my question was dismissed. I felt a little disheartened and unappreciated. I questioned why I was sacrificing so much if I was going to feel this way.
I left that meeting with no desire to attend the ward temple night. I called my wife, told her how discouraged I was, and said, “Let’s go to dinner instead of the temple.”
Linsey wisely responded, “No, I think you need to be in the temple. We’ll talk after.”
So I went to the temple, but not with the best attitude.
As I entered the dressing room, grumbling to myself, I heard someone say, “How are you, brother?”
It was Elder Dallin H. Oaks.
We had never met before, and I wasn’t about to tell a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles how discouraged I felt. So I forced a smile and said, “Everything’s great!”
I changed into my temple clothes, and as I walked out, to my surprise, Elder Oaks was waiting for me.
He said, “Brother, tell me how you are really doing.”
Something about the compassion in his voice helped me open up. Elder Oaks listened. He expressed sincere gratitude, said some encouraging words, and even answered my administrative question. Then he gave me a big hug, and in an instant I went from feeling like giving up to feeling like I could give my whole soul in service to the Lord.
Five years later, my wife and I were invited to meet with Elder Oaks in his office. You can imagine my excitement to reminisce about the experience we had shared. I asked him, “Do you remember the conversation we had in the temple?”
“I don’t think so,” he said. “Have we met before?”
I recounted the experience and reminded him how his act of compassion had lifted my spirits and changed my life.
Elder Oaks responded, “I’m sorry, brother. I don’t remember that.” Then, sensing my disappointment, he added, “But it’s what we do. Isn’t it?”
Those words have stayed with me ever since. That is what we do. As covenant followers of Jesus Christ, we minister with compassion to whomever God places in our path. We do it because that’s what the Savior did. And we’ve made a covenant to follow Him.

A Covenant of Compassion

Each Sabbath day, when you and I partake of the sacrament, we witness to our Father in Heaven our willingness to take upon ourselves the name of His Son, Jesus Christ. That means we choose to see as He sees, feel as He feels, and do as He would do. His life should be reflected in ours. It means that when someone encounters us, they should experience something of Jesus Christ—His kindness, His patience, His hope, His love, His compassion.
Our promise of willingness is met by the Lord’s promise that we can always have His Spirit with us. With that gift, we can minister as the Savior would, with His power and His loving kindness.
We make the covenant during sacred time with God every Sunday. A way we keep the covenant is by ministering to God’s children every day. Often this happens when God places someone in our path and we have eyes to see them. I call these “divine appointments.”

Eyes to See

When Jesus was asked, “What shall I do to inherit eternal life?” He answered with a story about a man who had eyes to see. In the story, a traveler lay wounded on the road to Jericho. Where others saw an inconvenience or an interruption, one man saw an opportunity to minister—a divine appointment. Seeing awakened compassion. Compassion moved him to act. And his actions changed a life forever.
This pattern defined the Savior’s ministry. He turned ordinary encounters with people into extraordinary moments of healing, encouragement, and transformation. To Jesus, these people were not interrupting His mission. They were His mission.
God has given us eyes to see. When we use them, we begin to recognize divine appointments all around us. What once looked like random encounters become invitations from the Lord to minister with compassion.
That’s what the Savior did. It’s what His prophet does. And it’s what we do, isn’t it?

Minister to the One God Places in Your Path

A few years ago, my wife and I were waiting to board a flight for a much-needed vacation. We arrived at the airport early, and I put my earbuds in and started reading a book, thankful for a few quiet moments to myself.
Before long, I glanced up and saw a young missionary sitting across from me. He looked frightened and anxious. His eyes were closed, he was rocking back and forth, and tears were streaming down his cheeks. Clutched in his hands were his boarding pass and a digital alarm clock.
After briefly imagining the various reasons a missionary might look so anxious, I returned to my book. But the Spirit prompted me to look again.
When I did, I saw his tear-filled eyes looking at me, pleading for help.
“Are you OK?” I asked.
In broken, timid English, he explained that he was on the way to his mission, it was going to be his first time on an airplane alone, and he was terrified. I learned he was a long way from his home country and he was holding the alarm clock to make sure he didn’t miss the plane.
Embarrassed by how slow I had been to help this elder, I explained that my wife and I would be on the same flight, and we would make sure he made it on the plane.
Linsey and I walked him to the gate and showed him the door he would go through. Soon it was our turn to board, so Linsey and I left him at the gate and took our seats.
As the plane filled up, we anxiously watched for our missionary friend, but there was no sign of him. I worried we had made a big mistake by boarding without him.
Finally, there he was—like every missionary, the last one to board—still clutching his boarding pass and alarm clock, making his way toward the only empty seat, at the back of the plane.
It was the seat next to me.
We smiled at each other, amazed at how God had arranged even a small detail like that one. Then the elder, finally relaxing a bit, fell fast asleep.
When we landed, I woke him, and the panic returned to his face as he worried about what to do next. Where was he supposed to go? What if there was no one waiting for him?
Linsey and I helped him get off the plane and walked him, arm in arm, not to lose him again, all the way to the baggage claim area. Waiting for him there were his mission leaders. Knowing what a special moment this always is, we were excited to see this new missionary being greeted by his leaders for the very first time.
But to our surprise, our friend didn’t run to his mission leaders. Instead, he dropped his bags and gave Linsey and me a big hug of love and appreciation.
What we did for that elder didn’t require much of us, but this ordinary encounter became a divine appointment we will always treasure. All we had to do was see the person God had placed in our path, look with compassion rather than judgment, and then act.
Brothers and sisters, let us pray every day for eyes to see the divine appointments God places before us! Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us. It’s what Jesus did.
And it’s what we do.
In the sacred name we take upon ourselves by covenant, even Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Christian C. Chigbundu
title: Spiritual Immunity
content:
In 2020 the world experienced a global health crisis that not only grounded economic activities but also claimed millions of lives around the world. During this period, executives at my place of work, in a bid to provide awareness and safety, invited health professionals to provide health education on COVID-19 and ways to prevent infection. Throughout these health sessions, there was one recurring word: immunity.
I learned that immunity is the body’s inherent biological ability to defend and protect itself against infectious diseases, harmful substances, and foreign invaders.
During this period I reflected not on my physical immunity but on what I call “spiritual immunity.” I pray for the help of the Holy Ghost as we consider some of the ways to build our spiritual immunity.
We live in troubled times marked by wars, family challenges, and economic uncertainty. Yet, as frightening as these challenges may be, we need not fear! As we build our spiritual immunity, we develop the strength and courage to withstand the challenges of life.
President Henry B. Eyring said: “[Proving] moments are not evidence that the Lord has abandoned you. Rather, they are evidence that He loves you enough to refine and strengthen you” (“Proved and Strengthened in Christ,”, Nov. 2025, 95).
As you listen today, think for a moment: What keeps you awake at night or weighs on your mind? Know that the Lord has provided us with a spiritual compass to help us navigate life’s challenges. This I call “small and simple things.” Alma taught his son Helaman in the Book of Mormon, “By small and simple things are great things brought to pass” (Alma 37:6).
May I share some of these small and simple things with you?
First, scripture study. When we study the scriptures, we get knowledge, but more important, we come to know the Lord. As we apply what we learn, His words begin to shape how we think and how we respond to life challenges. The counsel of King Benjamin to his sons rings true:
“O my sons, I would that ye should remember that these sayings are true, and also that these records are true. …
