“And now, my sons, I would that ye should remember to search them diligently, that ye may profit thereby” (Mosiah 1:6, 7).
Daily, meaningful scripture study invites the guidance of the Holy Ghost and builds our faith to face the temptations and the troubles of the world.
While serving as mission leader, I received a new missionary. In our welcome interview, this young missionary began to cry and asked to be sent home. When I asked why, he couldn’t find the right words to explain. Then I asked him if he had a testimony of the Book of Mormon. He said, “President, I don’t.”
I bore my testimony of the Book of Mormon and then encouraged him to begin to study the scriptures, especially the Book of Mormon. He and his trainer made a scripture study plan. Later I received a letter from this missionary testifying of how daily scripture study had helped him understand his purpose as a missionary. He said, “I am happy now and do not want to be sent home any longer.”
My dear friends, I invite you to search the scriptures diligently, that you might know the word of God (see Alma 17:2). As we do this, little by little we learn how to become lifelong disciples of Jesus Christ.
Second, prayer. Our Savior extended a remarkable invitation to all of us when He said, “Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me” (Doctrine and Covenants 88:63).
When we pray to our Heavenly Father, we draw near to Him and seek His help, guidance, and blessings.
There are many examples in the scriptures of people who experienced the enabling power and miracle of prayers: Enos, Nephi, the Prophet Joseph Smith, and the Savior Jesus Christ. They remind us of the power that comes when we turn to Heavenly Father in prayer.
While serving as an Area Seventy, I attended a stake conference in Côte d’Ivoire. After the Saturday adult session, the stake president and I decided to visit a sister who is battling with cancer. When we asked how she was feeling, she said something that remains with me to this day: “As I pray daily, I realize that the Savior loves me. I see His hands all around me, telling me, ‘My daughter, all is well.’”
As we pray in faith, our spiritual immunity will be strengthened. The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them (see Mosiah 24:14–15).
Third, the sacrament. The sacrament is a sacred ordinance that strengthens our relationship with the Savior.
During the sacrament we make promises to take upon us the name of Jesus Christ, to always remember Him, and to keep His commandments (see Doctrine and Covenants 20:77, 79). As we partake of the sacrament, we can ask ourselves, “What would He have me do?” As we remember Jesus Christ throughout the week and strive to keep His commandments, our lives are gradually refined and reshaped. Our “Why me?” questions will be replaced by “What can I learn, and what can I change?”
Fourth, covenants. Making covenants and staying on the covenant path are inseparable companions. Covenants create a bond between us and God, and staying on the covenant path brings the promised blessings that come with that bond. Worshipping in the Lord’s house, the temple, is vital to staying on the covenant path.
President Dallin H. Oaks taught, “As we honor those covenants by keeping [Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ’s] commandments and following Their plan of redemption, Their promised blessings enable us to soar to celestial heights” (“Following Christ,”, Nov. 2024, 24).
What a promise, my friends. Remember that trials may come, yet as we worship in the temple and remember our covenants, we receive personal direction from the Lord that will guide us along the covenant path.
My beloved brothers and sisters, I invite you to always remember scriptures, prayers, the sacrament, and covenants. While they may seem small and simple, they are truly the armor of God that will help us stand against the tactics of the devil!
I bear you my witness that we have a loving Father in Heaven, that Jesus Christ is our Savior and Redeemer. President Dallin H. Oaks is truly the mouthpiece of God on earth today. In the name of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Patricio M. Giuffra
title: Trusting the Lord Through Tithes and Offerings
content:
Before I was baptized into the Church, the missionaries taught me about tithes and offerings. After my baptism, through summer jobs, I had the opportunity to pay full tithes and fast offerings. However, at that time, I did not fully understand the meaning of the promises and blessings associated with obedience to this law.
It was not until my missionary service that I had the opportunity to teach this commandment and bear testimony of it. While serving in the Chile Osorno Mission, in the city of Puerto Montt, Elder Ruben Alvarez and I began teaching a woman who was about 70 years old and lived with her son, who was a member of the Church. She could not read and had difficulty retaining what we taught her, so we needed to repeat each lesson twice.
When we began teaching the law of tithing and the promised blessings that come to those who obey it, with great sadness she said to me, “Elder Giuffra, I clean houses and wash clothes for several families. What I earn is barely enough to pay the rent for the room where we live, buy a small amount of firewood to keep us warm, and provide some food. I don’t think I will ever be able to live the law of tithing because I will not have enough money to do so.”
We were deeply moved. Everything she said made sense from a worldly perspective. Although we bore testimony of the great blessings the Lord promises to those who obey this commandment, she insisted that she could not do it.
The next morning, I called my mission president, President Fernando Caballero, to seek his counsel. In my mind, I wondered whether the Lord might have an exception for someone in her circumstances.
President Caballero read to me the account of the widow’s mite and then said, “Elder Giuffra, you are no one to deny this sister the blessings of the law of tithing. There are no exceptions to this commandment.”
Those words became engraved upon my heart. My companion and I decided to pray and fast because two days later we would return to review the commandments once again before her baptism.
When we arrived at her home and began reviewing the lessons, we came once again to the law of tithing. She said to us, “Last night I knelt in prayer and told Heavenly Father that I truly wanted to become a member of His Church and that He would need to help me live this law.”
As we heard those words, a profound feeling of peace and assurance filled our minds and hearts. We knew that the Lord had heard both her prayers and ours.
She was baptized the following Saturday. A few weeks later, I was transferred to another area, but I remained in contact with her bishop. He told me she arrived every week with her tithing envelope and that on the first Sunday of every month she also brought her fast offering.
Throughout my life, I have learned to trust in the Lord, and I have seen innumerable blessings come to my family and me as we have sought to faithfully live the law of tithing and offerings. Some blessings have been temporal, others spiritual, but all have strengthened our testimony that the Lord always fulfills His promises and that the windows of heaven are opened according to our obedience.
My wife often teaches a principle that has become very meaningful in our family: We keep the commandments because we love God, not merely because we hope to receive the blessings that come from obedience. Commandments are given to draw us closer to the Savior, to protect us, and to help us remain free from sin and many of the challenges the world presents.
This does not mean that we will be free from trials or difficulties. All of us will face moments of uncertainty, financial hardship, illness, or loss. Yet even when we do not understand the purpose of our trials, we can have the assurance that the Lord knows our circumstances, honors our obedience, and fulfills His promises in His own time and way.
President Russell M. Nelson taught that “tithing can break cycles of poverty in poor nations and families.
“‘We preach tithing to the poor people of the world because the poor people of the world have had cycles of poverty, generation after generation,’ he said. ‘That same poverty continues from one generation to another, until people pay their tithing.’”
During my years of service in Central America, I have seen men and women prosper both temporally and spiritually. I have met families who once worried about their next meal but who now enjoy greater stability. I have known children of God who once could not afford a pair of shoes and who today, through faith and diligent effort, own successful businesses. I have also witnessed the Lord open doors for employment, provide education, strengthen marriages, and fill faithful hearts with peace and hope.
President Dallin H. Oaks taught: “The payment of tithing … brings the individual tithe payer unique spiritual blessings. Tithe paying is evidence that we accept the law of sacrifice. It also prepares us for the law of consecration and the other higher laws of the celestial kingdom.” These laws are fulfilled as we keep the covenants made in the house of the Lord, which deepens and perpetuates our relationship with Jesus Christ.
“Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings. …
“Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.”
I testify that the law of tithing is a law of faith. As we obey it, we demonstrate our trust in the Lord and allow Him to work miracles in our lives, often in ways we do not expect. Christ lives. This is His Church, and President Dallin H. Oaks is His prophet. In the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Jeremiah J. Morgan
title: The Infinite Power of God in Our Covenants
content:
When I was a young teenager getting ready for school, my mother read to me from the Book of Mormon every day, out loud, whether I was listening or not.
So, you might assume that I was raised in a family that belonged to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. But I was not. My family were members of a different church that also believes in the Book of Mormon and the prophetic mission of Joseph Smith. I am deeply grateful for that heritage, a heritage that began with my third-great-grandparents Francis and Mary Ann Case, who were baptized by Oliver Cowdery in 1831 and helped establish Nauvoo and build the house of the Lord.
They did not travel west with the Saints; nevertheless, I was raised with a knowledge and testimony of the Prophet Joseph Smith. My mother actually gave me my middle name, Joseph, after the Prophet of the Restoration. And she gave me much more than that. She taught me about the restored gospel and the Book of Mormon.
There are only two things I remember from that reading of the Book of Mormon by my mother: “and it came to pass” and “wars and rumors of wars.” That’s it.
But more than any words that I heard or did not hear, I knew the Book of Mormon was important to my mother. And I knew she knew it was true. Even as a single mother, she made the extraordinary effort to read the Book of Mormon to me every day until it was finished. As she did, she was fulfilling the admonition of the Lord, who said, “Remember the new covenant, even the Book of Mormon.”
The lesson I learned is this: No time or effort is ever wasted in reading the Book of Mormon. Not for you, not for your children, not for your family, not for anyone.
Because of my mother’s extraordinary efforts, I knew the Book of Mormon was true and that Joseph Smith was a prophet of God. Even so, I was confused and uncertain as to where the true Church of Jesus Christ was. When I was 14, I began to question the church of my childhood. I knew members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; they were my friends.
All of this led me to sincerely seek the truth. So, for two months I attended both my family’s congregation, and secretly—hiding between the accordion doors of the overflow—I attended a congregation of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. I can’t fully express the gratitude I have for my upbringing and the knowledge I had received; even so, I came to know that this is the Lord’s Church.
It would be some time before I could join the Church, and though I would face questions and disappointment from my family, I had been given a gift—a testimony. And in the words of the Prophet Joseph Smith, “I knew it, and I knew that God knew it, and I could not deny it.”
I was retelling this experience and pondering how a young boy such as me would have an interest in religion. There were many good influences in my life, to be sure, but that did not seem to explain it all. While I was musing out loud about this topic, my wife, Rebecca, said, “I know what it was! It was covenants.”
You see, while my ancestors were united with the Saints in Nauvoo, they had made covenants in the temple. Rebecca then read some of the beautiful and comforting prophetic teachings on this topic, which provide that because of “the eternal sealings of faithful parents and the divine promises made to them[,] … though some of the sheep may wander, the eye of the Shepherd is upon them, and sooner or later they will feel the tentacles of Divine Providence reaching out after them and drawing them back to the fold.”
It was covenants; I felt it in that moment. And in these words, we begin to feel a sense of the awesome power of God in our covenants.
President Dallin H. Oaks has said that covenants “do not ‘take a day off.’”
Though the covenant faithfulness of parents and grandparents does not alter the agency of children or grandchildren, there is a discernible impact of those covenants on all our posterity.
It was covenants that had impacted me, not my covenants but the covenants of those who came before me. The power of God in those covenants reached out after me. As Elder Patrick Kearon has taught, “He employs every possible measure to bring [us] back.”
It is exactly how the Lord revealed it to the Prophet Joseph Smith: “And he shall plant in the hearts of the children the promises made to the fathers, and the hearts of the children shall turn to their fathers.”
We can see this promise being fulfilled in our day. In the Book of Mormon, the Lord made a covenant with Enos that the remnant of the people living at that time would someday receive his words and the fulness of the gospel of Jesus Christ. Was there a time limit to that covenant? That covenant would take more than 2,000 years to be fulfilled. So, no, there is no limit to the power of God in our covenants.
Covenants with God are filled with incalculable power. They do not bless just the maker of the covenant but are generational in their impact. We are all the intended beneficiaries of countless covenants! Like the great binding power of gravity that stretches across the universe, covenants with God stretch over all time and all space.
If you are wondering whether you or a loved one has wandered so far away that the love of God and His covenantal power cannot reach you—I say to you, you have not. As President Jeffrey R. Holland so beautifully said: “You have not traveled beyond the reach of divine love. It is not possible for you to sink lower than the infinite light of Christ’s Atonement shines.”
The Atonement of Jesus Christ is the fulfillment of the greatest promise God made—that Jesus Christ would be our Savior and Redeemer. The power and reach of that covenant is infinite and eternal.
Some may be crying out right now, with words like “O, God, where art Thou? My child is struggling.” Take comfort; God hears you and will answer your prayers in His own time and in His own way. Keep your covenants, strive to be faithful, and “cheerfully do all things that lie in [your] power; and then may [you] stand still, with the utmost assurance, to see the salvation of God, and for his arm to be revealed.”
I testify that the infinite power of God is in our covenants. Don’t ever give up. Your story, your family’s story, is not all written. God is the author and the finisher of it. I am a standing, breathing, believing demonstration of God’s love and the power of God in covenants. Blessed be the name of the Lord, of whom I testify in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Hutch U. Fale
title: I Am a Child of God
content:
I am a child of God and He loves me. This statement is powerful and empowering. More importantly, it is true, not just for me but for each of us and all of us.
“All human beings—male and female—are created in the image of God. Each is a beloved spirit son or daughter of heavenly parents, and, as such, each has a divine nature and destiny. …
“In the premortal realm, spirit sons and daughters knew and worshipped God as their Eternal Father and accepted His plan [for] His children.”
I bear solemn witness of the reality of this “plain and precious” truth, powerful and simple. Understanding our Father’s love and our true identity as His children is essential for our daily and eternal happiness. It prevents deception and gives purpose to this mortal life.
The divine pattern of families teaches us of our Father’s love and our relationship to Him. In fact, “our relationship to God … [is] explained in terms of the family.” Holy scriptures also teach us in terms of the family. The New Testament begins with a young family and a baby born in Bethlehem. The Book of Mormon begins with a family’s journey of faith, and the Old Testament teaches how the Creation was not complete until God had organized a family. It is often through families, despite all their imperfections, that our Father teaches us about His love.

While at a Church meeting last year, I received an impression to do what the teacher was doing. So, in a text, I asked my wife to find a baby picture of each of our children. When I got home, we sat down and showed my kids their pictures. I told them that there are no words to fully express the love we felt when they were born, including the day each picture was taken. I then asked, “As of the date of this picture, what had you done to earn our love?” They lowered their eyes and said, “Nothing.” I asked them to look up and said, “You are right. You did nothing to earn our love. By that same token, there is nothing you can ever do that will unearn or remove that love from you. You did not earn it; you cannot lose it. It is yours forever.”
I continued, “We need you to always remember that what we feel is but a small fraction of what your Heavenly Father feels for you. You are His child and He loves you. He loved you before you were born, He loves you today, and He will love you tomorrow. He wants you to prepare to be like Him. You must never forget this. We hope this understanding gives you courage to do your best, to trust Him, and to live up to your potential. We also hope it gives you the strength and the humility to come home when you need to, because no matter what has happened, you can always come home, just as you can always turn to your Father in Heaven.” There were tears and tender hearts as the Holy Spirit bore witness that this was true.
I referenced my children, but for you it might be a special love for siblings, parents, spouse, aunts, uncles, a grandparent you never met before. Or maybe all that is there is a desire for a family or for healthy family-like relationships. Families evidence a divine and eternal pattern, connecting us to our Eternal Father and to His eternal family. Even when a loving family is not part of our earthly experience, knowing that our Heavenly Father loves us can provide power, peace, and comfort, especially as we remember the eternal blessings that await all who make and keep sacred covenants—including all the blessings of an eternal family.
As I bear witness of the eternal depth and nature of our Father’s love, I also offer this warning: Beware of the adversary’s deceitful lie that twists this precious truth. He tries to deceive God’s children into believing that because God loves us, we can be saved regardless of our pride, regardless of our rebellion, regardless of our sins, and regardless of our rejection of His Son and His Son’s servants. Receiving Christ through priesthood ordinances and covenants, and then being faithful to those covenants, is the only way for us to fully understand His love and the only way to exaltation.
Knowing and understanding our Father’s love is important for many reasons. I will share just three.
First, understanding our Father’s love helps us better understand Jesus Christ. We better understand why He did what He did and why He loves us the way He does. We recognize why He is anxiously engaged in trying to save and bless all of His Father’s children. This understanding makes us eager to quickly and wholeheartedly join Him in His Father’s work. As we are anxiously engaged in this work, we are able to become more like Him.
Second, when we understand God’s love for us and for the rest of His children, we become immune to the divisive and misleading labels of our fallen world, both the labels that people try to put on us and the labels the world tries to put on others. We see ourselves and all of God’s children as beloved and divine. We become quick to repent, slow to judge, and ever hopeful that the best is yet before us. We are forever willing to love and to make sure that no one is ever sitting, standing, or walking alone.
Third, understanding our Father’s love protects us from the pernicious lie that it is too late for someone to change, too late for someone to turn to Christ, and too late to receive His redeeming grace. From the prodigal son to leaving the 99 sheep to find the one, our Father’s message, through His Son, has always been that there is still yet time if we turn to Christ today.
God’s love is real, and Jesus Christ is evidence of that love. To fulfill His divine responsibility to help His Father’s children, He conquered sin and the grave. While still a mortal, He taught us to pray to “our Father.” Not just His Father, not someone else’s father, but our Father—a loving Heavenly Father who gives better gifts to His children than any other earthly father gives to his. Jesus Christ, through His premortal, mortal, and current ministry, points us to eternal life and personifies our Father’s deep, abiding, and eternal love.
Today Christ shows us our Father’s love through priesthood keys held by living prophets and apostles. These priesthood keys allow access to sacred ordinances and covenants that prepare us to return to our Father. Living prophets and apostles stand as witnesses that the resurrected Christ is evidence of the continuing and immeasurable love of our Eternal Father.
What I witness before you today first came by way of the Holy Spirit when I was a young boy riding from Nuku‘alofa to my home village of Mu‘a. I was reading a copy of the New Testament that referenced John 3:16 in several different languages: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” I knew this was true then, and I know it is true now.
Jesus is the Christ. He, His restored Church, and the divine pattern of families stand as witnesses of our Father’s love.
I, Hutch ‘Ungapapalangi Fale, am a child of God. He loves me and He loves you. May this truth never leave our minds or our hearts, and may it change us forever. In the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Patrick Kearon
title: Jesus Lives to Lift
content:
A few weeks ago, President Dieter F. Uchtdorf took me aside and said, “Patrick, your talks—they’re OK, but where is the aviation?” So here’s just a little aviation.

My Early Ambition

I spent much of my childhood at boarding school in England looking up at aeroplanes crossing the sky, dreaming of flying home to my parents thousands of miles away in Arabia. I yearned to fly! I wanted to become a fighter pilot.

The Basics of Learning to Glide

The Royal Air Force was recruiting pilots, and the fastest way for me to fly was learning to glide.
A glider is a lightweight aircraft with long, slender wings—and no engine—that stays aloft by riding within rising currents of air.

So in my mid-teens I spent part of two summers at an airfield in Oxfordshire learning to fly a glider with the air force. First I learned to fly “straight and level,” then to make stable turns, next to take off towed by a tug plane, and finally to land safely back at the airfield. Only then was I ready to learn to stay in the air, climb, and eventually soar—all without an engine!

Lift

The crucial skill in gliding is finding rising air. You cannot see it, but you can see what it does. I was taught to look for cumulus clouds because they often mark where warm air is rising, and I learned to fly toward them.
But even more important than using visual cues to find rising air is to learn to feel it. While flying along, I would begin to feel that I was being lifted by an unseen force. This rising air is called “lift.” One wing would tip upward, and I would turn toward it, into the lift.

I was taught how to stay in lift, circling upward to gain altitude, and to often join other pilots who had found lift, climbing with them in the same invisible column of rising air.
To be flying is fantastic, but climbing in lift and soaring with no engine is almost beyond description. For me it was beautiful—with only the whistle of the wind, the occasional creak from the glider, and the magnificent sensation of being drawn upward!

Sink

Just as there is rising air, there is also sinking air, called “sink.” It likewise cannot be seen, but it can be felt, and I quickly learned to avoid it. Gliding into sink can feel like falling, sometimes quickly. It shortens the distance you might fly and may threaten a safe landing. When I encountered sink, I learned to turn away decisively.

Our Saviour Loves to Lift

A decade after those gliding days, and not far into my journey of faith, I recognised that the principles of gliding I had learned in my teens have significant similarities with spiritual principles: We must avoid sink and find lift.
At the heart of our faith is the glorious truth that we have an adoring Father in Heaven, whose Son, our Saviour, loves to lift!Just think of all the scriptural accounts that show our Redeemer lifting people from despair, out of their figurative “sink.” With His all-powerful hand, He lifted His beloved Peter from sinking in the waves; He lifted the daughter of Jairus from the depths of death; and after healing the boy plagued with an unclean spirit who “was as one dead; … Jesus took him by the hand, and lifted him up.”
Our Saviour constantly sought out the most desperate souls sinking into darkness and dread and lifted them up. And He wants to lift you!

We Can Learn to Avoid Spiritual Sink and Find Spiritual Lift

Through the amazing grace of Jesus Christ, we can avoid spiritual sink and find spiritual lift. Spiritual lift cannot be seen, but as we learn to discern and act upon the sensitive impressions of the Holy Spirit, we can feel it—as surely as I felt the rising air lift a wing beneath me.
Can you identify moments when you have felt undeniable spiritual lift? Where were you? How did it feel? Isn’t it magnificent to feel like you are being drawn upward, rising higher and higher toward your Heavenly Father and your intended eternal potential?
Can you likewise identify moments when you have felt spiritual sink? You likely remember how this felt in contrast. Just as with gliding, we turn away from it decisively.

If You Aren’t Rising in Lift, You Are Descending

In gliding, if you are not actively climbing in lift, you are descending. This is an uncomfortable fact. A descent can be so gradual that, unless you watch your altitude, you may not notice you are sinking.
Isn’t it the same in our lives? How easy it is to slowly slip from spiritual heights we have worked so hard to climb when we neglect the practices and behaviours that brought us there. We rarely intend to sink. We want lift—its joy and blessings—but we may not recognise the quiet cost of neglecting vital communion with our Father, Saviour, and the Holy Spirit.

Experiencing Lift

When we first experience spiritual lift, it is wondrous. We may feel a soul-expanding lightness of being unlike anything we’ve ever experienced.
A compelling example of this in the Book of Mormon is when Ammon praises God for “[loosing his] brethren from the chains of hell.” They had been “encircled about with everlasting darkness and destruction” and were then “brought … into … everlasting light, … encircled about with the matchless bounty of [God’s] love”—redemption from the ultimate sink to the ultimate lift!
Ammon then tries to express his thanksgiving: “Behold, who can glory too much in the Lord? Yea, who can say too much of his great power, and of his mercy, and of his long-suffering towards the children of men? Behold, I say unto you, I cannot say the smallest part which I feel.”
Ammon cannot begin to describe this profound transition from devastating sink to the most glorious lift. And I haven’t met anyone who can. The language of the Spirit of God is not a language of words.

Staying in Lift

But lift and sink in the spiritual realm are nevertheless real. Pay close attention to the sweet, peaceful feelings that come when you choose spiritual lift, the rising forces that bring you into the Saviour’s loving upward pull.
Likewise, pay attention to the dim and dampening feelings that lead away from the Redeemer and His infinite love.
And oh! the joy that comes when others experience lift, circling upward with us in the love and light of Jesus Christ! As children of the covenant, we are privileged with the responsibility of assisting the Lord in fulfilling His promises to all His children. Helping others turn from sink and into the lift of Jesus Christ is our glorious opportunity and brings joy beyond compare.

Jesus Christ Lives and Loves to Lift

We can learn to live in spiritual lift. And when we sink, our gentle Saviour is there to lift us up as we turn to Him. Jesus Christ loves to lift!
What does living in lift actually look like? A few simple things. Find a faithful guide and learn from them where lift is found. Actively tune in to the sweet feelings of the Holy Spirit and the things in your life that lead you there. Join those who are climbing. Do what they do. Watch closely for the subtle signs of sink in your own life, and turn away decisively. And when you find lift yourself, show someone else where and how to rise! Then soar in the joy of the Lord!
The Saviour’s promise is “If ye do these things blessed are ye, for ye shall be lifted up at the last day.”
None of this is complicated; we simply need to keep turning toward the Saviour, into the source of lift, and keep choosing to rise into the light rather than drift imperceptibly into the shadow.
Remember: our Father sent His magnificent Son to be lifted up upon the cross that thereby He might draw all of us into His loving embrace.
Your Saviour is your lift. He is your ever-rising air. There is no limit to how high you can climb with Him. Jesus Christ lives to lift. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Michael A. Dunn
title: The Ninety and Ten
content:
Among the myriad nearly incomprehensible blessings of our Savior Jesus Christ is His promise to carry our burdens. But what does that look like in practical terms—especially when we are weighed down and seemingly without hope?
Years ago I came to better understand how the Savior ministers to us in even more personal, profound, and private ways than I ever thought possible.
That realization came in 1998 when, in one of my very weak moments, my running partner Ted somehow talked me into entering a 100-mile (161-km) ultramarathon race. Clearly, I was not only out of my league but possibly out of my mind for saying yes. Sure, I’d run a few marathons before, but not four of them back-to-back.
Everything about it seemed impossible—except for one thing, and that was that Ted believed I could do it. That mattered because he had completed the race himself many times. He knew every twist of the trail and promised that if I would put in the training, he would be there to run with me through the second half of the race when fatigue, blisters, and especially self-doubt would become my worst enemies.
Race day arrived. Setting off in the predawn hours, I quickly realized this was bigger than me. But somehow I kept moving, even through the withering heat of the afternoon, one slogging step at a time. Then, with more than half the race ahead of me, and with daylight and my hopes fading, sure enough, Ted showed up.

With Ted’s patience and persistence and my unceasing silent prayers, we miraculously ran—make that trudged—to mile 90. Morning had barely dawned. Just 10 miles remained. But I was completely sapped—running on empty, as it were. Collapsing in the shade of a tree, I looked over at Ted and quietly said, “I give up.”
But even as my resignation settled in, I got what you could arguably call the world’s first-ever “Ted Talk”!
In a gentle, reassuring tone, he reminded me of the months of preparation and those early-morning runs. He then kneeled down, looked me in the eye, and said something I will never forget: “I know you can do this, Mike, and I’m going to get you there.”
Those simple, sincere words sparked something inside me. After a few more minutes, I got to my feet. At first I walked, then hobbled into, well, a pretty solid shuffle. And somehow, step by step, together we conquered those last 10 miles.
The impossible now looked possible. But about a hundred yards (91 m) from the finish line, Ted suddenly reached out and grabbed my hand.
“Congrats, man,” he said. “You did it!” And with that, he began to peel off even as I begged him to finish beside me. But he simply smiled and added, “This is your race to finish.” Which I somehow managed to do.
A week or so later, a photograph from the race arrived in the mail. Miraculously, a friend captured that exact moment when Ted and I parted ways. But it also revealed a startling secret.

As I looked closer, I saw what Ted really did for me that day.
Much to my astonishment, I saw that he wasn’t only carrying his water; he was carrying two of my water bottles and my pack—which he dutifully toted every step of those last 10 grueling miles.

Somehow, there on the side of the trail, with me in deep despair and ready to quit, he quietly lightened my load—strapping my hydration pack to his own waist. Without fanfare or fuss, he simply shouldered my heaviest burden.
As I marveled at his benevolence, my thoughts immediately turned to an infinitely more amazing load-bearing Friend, our Savior Jesus Christ, who, as Isaiah unequivocally assured, has “borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows,” which I assumed meant the trails we travel would somehow become easier. But as I’ve come to learn through this race and the ups and downs of my life, He simultaneously lifts and uplifts, sometimes in unseen fashion, multiplying and magnifying even our most minuscule offerings. In other words, the Redeemer rescues not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride.
Anytime we turn to Christ, we turn a corner. By His grace we can trust and expect His constant care. And because God knows our prayers even before we ask Him, it’s reasonable to assume that blessings may often materialize in the selfsame moment we verbalize. His grace, which is a duality defined as a “divine means of help or strength,” can free us from the freight we would otherwise carry. And even when we don’t perceive Him at our side, He enlists the Teds—both of this world and sometimes even the Teds beyond—with His heartening promise of angels all around us to bear us up.
One of the main reasons I trusted Ted during the race is the same reason we can implicitly trust Jesus in every aspect of our lives. Because He “marked the path and led the way,” there is no portion of our mortal sojourn He has not trod. He not only knows the road; He knows you and what you, as noble offspring of the divine, are capable of.
To those at or nearing their “mile 90,” ferrying the unimaginable, or if you feel like I did, both depleted and defeated, I promise that as you expend even your last drops of energy to ask, His helping hand will ultimately give you that much-needed leg up. And even when the outcome or the timing is not what you plead for, take solace knowing that feeling broken does not mean you’ve been abandoned by God.
Or, as President Dieter F. Uchtdorf taught: “Often the deep valleys of our present will be understood only by looking back on them from the mountains of our future experience. Often we can’t see the Lord’s hand in our lives until long after the trials have passed.”
Through “him who is mighty to save,” you will find “strength beyond [your] own.” In other words, don’t confuse the perceived invisibility of the Lord’s hand with the inveterate nature of the Lord’s heart. Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.
All these years later, when I glance at that photo and ponder the metaphorical “last 10 miles” I still often face in this sojourn called life, I’m reminded that sometimes the God who makes the impossible possible can part seas and move mountains. Other times He simply sends us a Ted. But most often He tops off our courage, capacity, and confidence by empowering us to “lay aside every weight” so we can “run with patience the race that is set before us.” In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Matthew J. Eyring
title: Comfort from the Holy Ghost
content:
Recently a friend of mine received a call from his wife informing him that their young married son had unexpectedly passed away the night before. He told me a single thought came to his mind at that moment: “I can’t fix this.”
We are trained from a young age to solve problems, to be independent, to have perseverance and resilience. But our apparent self-reliance masks a deeper reality: All of us, regardless of experience, talent, or willpower, will sooner or later encounter burdens we cannot possibly carry ourselves.
On another occasion we had the opportunity to go to dinner with a young couple who had recently lost one of their twins right before birth. It was the couple’s first pregnancy.
My wife and I went through a similar experience many years ago when she was preparing to deliver twins and one of them passed away before birth. As we sat at the table expressing empathy gained through our own suffering, we were grateful “to mourn with those that mourn … and comfort those that stand in need of comfort.” We spoke together of parenthood, feelings of loss, and the path to healing and hope.
Our mortal journey is designed to try our faith. Our challenges will be different depending on personal circumstance and even where we live in the world. I know that some of you worry about having enough food each day for you and your family. All of us face eventual limitations of physical or emotional health or the health of loved ones. We mourn when those close to us stray from the gospel path. We can be hurt by someone we love or hurt by the pain we have caused someone we love. We may feel misunderstood or deeply lonely. We might have a bad habit we’ve tried to overcome repeatedly without success.
It is important to not allow our challenges to negatively impact our faith. Our Savior, Jesus Christ, suffered for us. He knows exactly how we feel, especially in our darkest and most trying times. As you humbly turn to the Lord and cast your burdens on Him, you have His promise: “Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you.” He will provide comfort; He will provide answers on His timetable as you turn to Him. Answers will come by various means as guided by the Spirit, sometimes in the form of tools, resources, and help from other people. The Lord has promised:
“And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;
“Even the Spirit of truth; … for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.”
We have received repeated prophetic warnings that in coming days we will not survive spiritually without the constant influence of the Holy Ghost. One reason is that in a world of increasing temporal and spiritual turbulence, true sources of comfort will become more scarce. Without divine comfort, we risk losing hope; and without hope, we can lose our faith and stop trying. Our hearts can fail us.
There is hope in Jesus Christ.
President Dallin H. Oaks said recently: “I wonder if we fully appreciate the enormous significance of this belief in a literal, universal resurrection. The conviction that death is not the conclusion of our identity changes the whole perspective of our mortal life. It affects how we look on the physical challenges of mortality. It gives us the strength and perspective to endure the mortal challenges faced by each of us and by those we love. It signifies that mortal deficiencies are only temporary! It also gives us the courage to face our own death or that of loved ones—even deaths we might call premature.”
Do we truly appreciate all the Lord has done for us? He spares us from the only two things that can bring us permanent misery: separation from our bodies and separation from God because of sin. Even as He comforts us through temporary times of challenge and pain, He has prepared our rescue from permanent tragedy.
Jacob, in the Book of Mormon, taught: “O how great the goodness of our God, who prepareth a way for our escape from the grasp of this awful monster; yea, that monster, death and hell, which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit.”
Someday we will more fully realize how generous and kind the Lord has been to each of us. We will better understand and appreciate the depth of the Savior’s sacrifice and the reality that He and the Father are truly givers of good gifts.
“Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.” We will realize that all the suffering that brought us closer to the Savior was preparing us for greater blessings.
While in the hospital following the loss of the young couple’s twin baby, the new mother received a priesthood blessing. The husband, however, did not. After our dinner together, I had the opportunity to give this grieving father a priesthood blessing. Through the whisperings of the Spirit, he was promised peace “which passeth all understanding” during this difficult time and throughout his life. As he and his wife left that evening, their countenances shone with the light of the One in whom we must all put our complete trust.
The Savior’s peace is made manifest through the comforting power of the Holy Ghost. That comfort will help us when we go through the inevitable hardships of life and times when we can’t fix things on our own. Living worthy of the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost should be one of our highest priorities.
I bear my witness that Jesus Christ lives. May we forever place our faith and hope in Him and believe and find comfort in His promise: “I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.” In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Ronald A. Rasband
title: Love Like Jesus
content:
My dear brothers and sisters, my message is for everyone whose heart aches for loved ones who have turned away from the Lord, stepped away from obedience to God’s laws, breached their covenants, and left behind a string of broken hearts, becoming, as the Bible says, “tossed to and fro.”
As the Apostle Paul described, you may feel “burdened excessively,” beyond your strength, weighed down as if being “pressed out of measure.” If I asked for a show of hands of how many feel that way, hands would shoot up in this hall and around the world. Most of us have faced such anguish in our families or circle of friends. I know Sister Rasband and I have.
In our grief, we continuously ponder the whys, hows, and what ifs. We feel we have failed. We spend sleepless nights going over how we tried to draw our loved ones close to Jesus Christ and the Spirit. We preach, cajole, argue, demand, lecture, ignore, sit them down to watch general conference, and even send them links to the talks, like this one, but to no avail. If anything, these efforts can cause a greater rift.
By divine design, brothers and sisters, everyone must choose for themselves to follow Jesus Christ.
The Book of Mormon prophet Lehi viewed in a dream “numberless concourses of people … pressing forward” to the tree of life, which is the love of Jesus Christ. But “there arose a mist of darkness,” and some “wandered off,” setting up residence in the growing skyline of great and spacious buildings. The adversary’s deceit leads to confusion and misery. He can promise no life eternal, no life with God the Father, and no peace. Not now. Not ever!
How do we reset the clock while the adversary works overtime to destroy God’s plan of happiness?
Gratefully, the answer is in the Old Testament: “Be not afraid nor dismayed … ; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.”
Listen carefully. I ask you to turn over to Jesus Christ your despair for those wayward souls. We cannot change their hearts, but He can; He is a God of miracles. We love our family members and friends profoundly, but they are foremost children of our Father in Heaven, who knows and loves them even more than we do. Our Father, the great Elohim, gave His Beloved Son the authority and power necessary to heal all His children. That is the good news of the gospel. By the power of Jesus Christ’s Atonement, there is always a way back!
By His Atonement from the Garden of Gethsemane to the cross on Golgotha, He paid for the sins and bore the disappointments that wrack their souls and yours.
In the vernacular, Jesus Christ says to all who grieve, “I’ve got this!”
Jesus Christ is the perfect embodiment of love. Love is the centerpiece of His gospel and the essence of being like Him. Love can positively influence those who have strayed. The first great commandment is to “love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.” And the second great commandment is “Love thy neighbour as thyself.” As the Primary song says, “As I have loved you, love one another.”
Love is not stepping back or sanctioning others’ decisions and actions. Love is being interested in their lives, their successes, and their challenges. Love is being there with arms outstretched and a cheerful countenance. Love is lifting with faith and hope in our Lord and Savior. Love relies upon the calming influence of the Holy Ghost. The book of Proverbs teaches, “Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding … , and he [will] direct thy paths.” The path is marked by love.
President Dallin H. Oaks has counseled: “Let us avoid what is harsh and hateful. Let us seek to be holy, like our Savior.” That holiness comes when we are peacemakers, when we are charitable, patient, forgiving, and kind.
Love is expressed in prayer. In the Book of Mormon, Alma the Younger, talented and smooth-talking, “had rebelled against … God” and “had not kept his holy commandments.” An angel, “with a voice of thunder,” declared, “The Lord hath heard the prayers of his people, and also the prayers of his servant, Alma, who is thy father; for he has prayed with much faith concerning thee that thou mightest be brought to [a] knowledge of the truth … that the prayers of his servants might be answered according to their faith.” His father, Alma, had prayed for weeks, months, years, maybe decades.
For three long days and nights, young Alma “was racked with eternal torment.” Somewhere deep within came his father’s teachings of the coming of Jesus Christ “to atone for the sins of the world.” Alma cried in his heart, “O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me.” The love of the Savior filled him “with joy.” He became a mighty prophet and a major figure in the Book of Mormon.
“Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me,” our Savior says, “ … and ye shall find rest unto your souls.”
Brothers and sisters, Jesus Christ pulls more than His weight. His Atonement is witness of His all-encompassing love for each one of us. Brutal as it was for Him, His Atonement was crucial for our eternal journey. Remember, “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
He has already paid for the sins and errant choices of all of God’s children, including those for whom you and I grieve. He knows them. He knows their hearts; He loves them. He gave His very life to bring them home, all the way home.
Remember the prodigal son who chose to leave his safe moorings for “riotous living.” He lost his fortune and his self-respect, and he returned home in a wretched state.
“When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran [to him].” “He was lost” and now was “found.”
What brought him back? It was love. He knew where to find it. Love, brothers and sisters, is the answer to connecting with all of our loved ones. Our Father extends His protective arms to us and to those still distant from Him and His Son. He asks us to do the same. Jesus Christ beckons, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
I close with three suggestions to help us find rest:
First, let go of any guilt. We fail only when we give up and stop trying, so never, never give up on those you love. Remember the example of Alma praying for his son.
Second, follow the admonition of President Thomas S. Monson: “Never let a problem to be solved become more important than a person to be loved.”
Third, remember Jesus Christ is the answer. He is, always has been, and always will be. Seek Him through study of the scriptures and words of prophets, apostles, men and women leaders who are devoted to serving the Lord. And pray. Pray mightily to our Heavenly Father in the name of Jesus Christ. He will not leave us “comfortless.”
I promise you, as an Apostle of the Lord Jesus Christ, that when the devil sends “forth his mighty winds” pulling loved ones off course, “his mighty storm … shall have no power … to drag you down to the gulf of misery and endless wo, because of the rock upon which ye are built.” If that rock is Jesus Christ.
Trust Him. He’s got this! In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Henry B. Eyring
title: “Fear Not, I Am with Thee”
content:
My beloved brothers and sisters, I am grateful to be with you in this worldwide conference of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The hymn we just heard sung by the choir speaks of promises which will become more important and more precious in the time ahead for all of us and for those we love.
My message today is that the promises in that hymn are true. The lyrics, taken from the 41st chapter of Isaiah, have become a comforting guide for me, and they can be for you and for those you love in the trials which we individually face.
Let us listen again to those promises:

In ev’ry condition—in sickness, in health,
In poverty’s vale or abounding in wealth,
At home or abroad, on the land or the sea—
As thy days may demand, … so thy succor shall be.

Fear not, I am with thee; oh, be not dismayed,
For I am thy God and will still give thee aid.
I’ll strengthen thee, help thee, and cause thee to stand,
Upheld by my righteous, … omnipotent hand.

Those promises become more precious as we move through the challenges in our lives and in the lives of those we love. It is important to realize that the promise is not for the removal of challenges. My wise mother taught me that when I was a little boy. I had asked her, “Mother, why is life so hard?”
She smiled and said firmly, “Hal, of course it’s hard. It’s supposed to be. Life is a test.”
Years later I realized that as she spoke those words to me, she was passing through tests of her own and rising up through a lifetime of terrible medical trials. As a girl, she had been diagnosed with diseases that would cause lifelong health challenges. But because she knew the words “Fear not, I am with thee” were true, the Lord’s promise was fulfilled for her.
You might reasonably wonder why a loving and all-powerful God allows our mortal test to be so hard. It is because He knows that we must grow in spiritual cleanliness and stature to be able to live in His presence. To make that possible, Heavenly Father gave us a Savior and the power to choose for ourselves by faith to keep His commandments and to repent and to come unto Him.
The Savior not only understands and has felt grief, but He has “borne [your] griefs, and carried [your] sorrows.” He knows you perfectly. He knows your heart.
The combination of trials and their duration are as varied as are the children of our Heavenly Father. No two are exactly alike. But what is being tested is the same, at all times in our lives and for every person: Will we do whatsoever the Lord our God will command us?
As my mother went through her last days of life, she became bedridden. The only picture she had placed on her bedroom wall was of the Savior. It hung where she could see it as she lay in her bed.
My father had a cot placed next to her in the hospital room so that he could help her immediately during the nights. After she died, my father walked through the floor of the hospital ward to thank and to shake the hand of every nurse who had helped her.
Now, I tell that story to offer evidence that the Lord sends faithful disciples to help Him keep His promise to succor others in their distress. As President Spencer W. Kimball taught: “God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.”
The remainder of my message today is to thank those who have responded to the call to be the Lord’s servants to fulfill His promises to be with His children in their troubles. I wish to thank those who have helped Him and encourage others to join Him in keeping His promise today and in the hard days ahead.
I would like to share examples of what so many of you have already done and are doing to help the Lord fulfill His promise to succor those in need in His earthly kingdom. Many of you offer such consecrated service in a variety of ways.
You have prayed in faith consistently for your family members or friends to know who the Lord would have you help for Him. As a face or a name has come into your mind, you have reached out to them. Even your simple attention was a comfort. That you felt prompted to reach out to them was evidence to them that the Lord knew and loved them.
Many of you have recognized a discouraged missionary as an invitation to lift a servant of Jesus Christ. Wherever they serve, missionaries are being stretched and they are praying for strength. Whatever they are assigned to do, they are in need of encouragement.
Your kindness to them, even for a few seconds, or simply a warm smile can be a strengthening of their faith that the Lord is watching over them. When you speak to them, you will find words to build their faith that the Lord knows them and is aware of their circumstances.
Many of you have prayed regularly for the Lord’s servants in His Church in whatever calling they might hold. Every one of them is praying every day and every night to know what to do to better serve others and for strength to carry on.
You are an important part of the Lord’s answers to their prayers for assurance. As you show your appreciation and confidence in them that they have been inspired, they will feel evidence that God called them, knows them, and has guided and blessed them. They will be strengthened in their feeling of the Lord’s approval.
Another great opportunity can come when you invite the Holy Ghost to help you find ways to help the Lord comfort those who are pleading for it. The Book of Mormon prophet Alma taught: “As ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; … willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort.”
We know that the Lord will comfort all of those who try to follow Him. And He offers us the great blessing and trust to help Him keep His promise to succor Heavenly Father’s children in their tests along their mortal journey toward home.
That is a reason we shed tears of joy and take courage whenever we hear the words “Fear not, I am with thee,” and we are touched that He offers us the trust of helping and loving others.
I testify that this is His Church and that He keeps His promises, both through the Holy Spirit and through His loving, true, faithful disciples, in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Rosemary K. Chibota
title: A Child of God
content:
As a child, I learned that greetings in my culture communicate love, concern, respect, and belonging. My daughter recently reminded me of the significance of the southern African greeting sawubona, which means, “I see you.” This greeting is much more than a simple “hello.” It is an acknowledgment of another person’s worth and humanity. It communicates, “I recognize you. I respect you. You matter.”
The Savior Jesus Christ perfectly exemplified this principle. Throughout His ministry, He truly saw the people around Him. He saw the woman at the well, the leper, the blind man, and the child. Where others saw labels, He saw beloved sons and daughters of God. Even of the rich young man who later walked away from Him sorrowing, the scriptures say, “[And] Jesus beholding him loved him.”
One of my favorite sawubona moments in the Savior’s ministry occurred at the pool of Bethesda. There Jesus saw a man who had suffered with an infirmity for 38 years. Where others had walked past him for years, the Savior saw him, ministered to him, and healed him.
The good Samaritan also chose to see. Rather than allowing labels or differences to distract him, he saw a child of God in need and acted. The Savior’s example and the good Samaritan’s compassion are not beyond our reach. Often, helping others feel seen as children of God begins with something as simple as learning their name.
During our daughter’s final parent-teacher conference, a school janitor approached my husband and me. With tears in his eyes, he thanked us for our daughter. He explained that she regularly greeted him, knew his name, and even helped him clean up after lunch.
He told us, “Very few students know my name. Your daughter sees me.”
President Dallin H. Oaks reminded us that “all mortals are beloved children of God.” As mission leaders, we found that missionaries who understood and taught this truth were more effective in helping others come unto Christ.
I plead with you as disciples of Jesus Christ to pray to see others as He sees them and to treat them accordingly. Remember, “Jesus said love ev’ryone; treat them kindly too.” When we see others through the Savior’s eyes, love and service naturally follow. President Spencer W. Kimball taught, “God does notice us, and … it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.”
The Savior sees our divine potential and, as the scriptures teach, “calleth those things which be not as though they were.” He sees not only who we are but who we can become. Through His atoning sacrifice, He makes that divine potential possible for all of us.
Seeing others as children of God also influences the way we see ourselves, yet the world encourages us to see ourselves and others differently. The world invites us to focus on labels rather than eternal identity.
However, labels can never fully capture who we truly are. Living prophets have taught that our eternal identity matters far more than any worldly identifier. Our identity is not something we achieve; it is something we inherit as beloved sons and daughters of God.
Like many people, I have sometimes viewed myself through the lens of such labels. When President Oaks extended my new calling, he told me, “You’ve been called for who you are. The Lord knows you.” In that moment I was reminded that God’s view of us is always more complete and more hopeful than our own. This eased my feelings of inadequacy.
Whatever labels may weigh heavily upon you today, Jesus Christ can raise you above them. His grace is sufficient to lift you above every label and limitation.
Before we were students, athletes, employees, parents, citizens, or leaders, we were spirit children of our Heavenly Father. That eternal identity does not change when circumstances change, when we make mistakes, or when others misunderstand us. He loves you. He knows you. He sees you as you are now and sees who you will become. He has a plan for your life, and Jesus Christ is at the center of that plan!
President Russell M. Nelson taught us that embracing our divine identity influences every major decision in our lives. As we seek the Savior’s perspective, He will often guide us to those who need to be seen.
Years ago I prayed to know how I could help a coworker who seemed isolated. As I acted on simple promptings to include him, our friendship grew. I learned that when we ask Heavenly Father to help us see others, He guides us to those who feel unseen.
You too can make a difference in someone’s life today simply by seeing them and acknowledging them. Remember that every person has divine worth. When we see one another through the Savior’s eyes, hearts change, relationships deepen, and faith grows.
This week, I invite you to:

Learn the name of someone who may feel unseen.

Pray to see others as Heavenly Father sees them.

Replace worldly labels with these eternal truths: Child of God. Child of the covenant. Disciple of Jesus Christ.

My dear friends, I leave you a final sawubona. I see you. More important, your Heavenly Father sees you. Your Savior, Jesus Christ, sees you. They know your name, your circumstances, your gifts, and your divine potential.
As we learn to see ourselves and one another as They do, our homes, wards, schools, and communities will become places of belonging, healing, and love. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Neil L. Andersen
title: Courage Born of Our Faith in Jesus Christ
content:
We welcome President Rosemary Chibota to the general leadership of the Church. Her story is an example of courage born of faith in Jesus Christ.
Seventeen-year-old Rosemary found a Joseph Smith pamphlet missionaries had left at her home in Zimbabwe. She read it and immediately received a spiritual witness that it was true; Joseph had seen God the Father and His Son, Jesus Christ. She was taught and baptized and became an example to her parents, who joined the Church 19 years later.
Faith and courage are hallmarks of disciples of Jesus Christ.
Jesus Christ is the divine Son of God. He came to earth in the humblest of circumstances. He lived a perfect life. He taught us how to live our mortal lives and how to prepare for our eternal lives. Because of His incomparable love for each of us, He gave a gift only He could give, suffering for our sins, allowing us to repent and be forgiven. He was crucified on the cross and, in the majesty of our Heavenly Father’s plan, rose the third day. Because He rose from the tomb, we too will be resurrected. How sublime are the purposes of our God and how immense is our reverence for our Savior.

Spiritual Courage

Being His true disciple, overcoming the world, keeping His commandments, and trusting in Him and His promises are not casual pursuits. Spiritual courage is the triumph over obstacles, doubt, and fear in choosing the right.
It has always taken spiritual courage, born of faith in Jesus Christ, to be His disciple. “I am alone,” Moroni wrote. “My father [and all my family have] been slain in battle, … and I have not friends nor whither to go.”
Even as his adversaries were putting to death everyone who would not deny the Christ, in his courage he declared, “And I, Moroni, will not deny the Christ.”
Our world is different than Moroni’s day, but discipleship always requires courage. The doubts, distractions, and deceptions of our day can be described in the words of the Apostle Paul: “We wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world.”
Our world is in constant commotion. Our phone seems almost attached to our hand, bringing a flood of information, misinformation, and now artificial information.
I grew up on a small dairy farm. For a season our three dozen cows were housed near a small canyon. Nearly every summer morning after milking, I would saddle my horse and guide the cows into a high meadow to graze, with no cell phone, no earbuds, no music, no texting. All day long, just me and the cows, alone with my thoughts. Times have changed, but our spirits have not changed. We need stillness to nourish our faith in Christ.

Faith and Courage

As we choose faith in Christ, He blesses us with the courage, sometimes in very difficult situations, to choose the right, and as we manifest our courage to choose the right, our faith in Christ strengthens.
We rejoice in the faith in Jesus Christ and the spiritual courage we see in you, our members of the Church across the world.
It is our faith in Jesus Christ that gives us the desire to humbly kneel alone and pray to our Heavenly Father. In those quiet moments when we speak with our Heavenly Father privately, independently, we are given the increased courage to choose the right. As a young man, I heard President David O. McKay say, “The greatest battle of life is fought within the silent chambers of your own soul.” As we courageously win the battles of the soul, our faith in our Savior multiplies.
Each week we prayerfully receive the sacrament and witness before God, and in the presence of others, that we “are willing to take upon [ourselves] the name of [Jesus Christ], and always remember him and keep his commandments.” Then, with courage, we are true to our covenants, and in turn, the Lord blesses us with increased faith.
It is our faith in Jesus Christ that gives us the courage to accept a calling from our priesthood leaders even when we feel inadequate or without sufficient time to accept the responsibility.

As a young attorney, President Dallin H. Oaks was energetically working in a prestigious law firm, including working evenings and Saturdays. His stake president called him to be a counselor in the stake mission presidency, necessitating at least three to four evenings per week. President Oaks reflected, “Gathering all my faith, I accepted the call.” President Oaks described this as a very important decision in his life. His faith strengthened his courage, and his decision brought increasing faith.
It is our faith in Jesus Christ that brings the spiritual courage to minister to others, live the Word of Wisdom, keep the law of chastity, honor the Sabbath day, be honest in our tithing, and trust our Father and His Son when unforeseen illness, financial troubles, or natural disaster upend our life.

A month ago I accompanied President Dieter F. Uchtdorf to Spokane, Washington, where fires destroyed more than 800 homes. We visited members whose neighborhoods were completely destroyed. “Our family is safe,” Cody and Haylee Woodbury said to me, “and our faith is secure. We can build another house.” Their faith in Jesus Christ lifted their courage, and their courage has elevated their faith.
It is the faith of tens of thousands of remarkable young men and women across the world that gives them the courage to get up before the sun rises to attend seminary and then to serve missions and, upon returning, to marry and begin a family. And for those not able to marry, their courage helps them to remain true to their covenants.
With faith in Christ and remarkable courage, a young mother prepares her small children for church, knowing that some Sundays will be more a wrestle of survival than a spiritual renewal.
It is our faith in Christ that gives us the spiritual courage to speak openly with others about our Savior, make covenants in the house of the Lord, repent and receive forgiveness, follow living prophets, and be guided by the quiet impressions of the Holy Ghost.
Recently a noble woman of deep faith shared her testimony in church. Confidentially, I knew that she had been devastated by the betrayal of her husband. But with courage born of her faith, she powerfully declared that in happiness or unspeakable grief, she would trust in the rock of her salvation, her Savior, Jesus Christ.
With our hope alive in Christ, even with life’s challenges, we too may be, as the Apostle Paul said, “troubled on every side, yet not distressed; … perplexed, but not in despair.”

Promises and Testimony

I promise you that as you strengthen your faith in Jesus Christ by believing and following Him and keeping His commandments, your answers will come, your spiritual power will increase, and your courage in following Christ will define your eternal soul.

The Savior declared, “If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.”
Peter and John were in the room when the resurrected Christ appeared to the Apostles. “Behold my hands and my feet,” Jesus said, “that it is I myself: handle me, and see.”
Soon after this sacred experience, disbelieving rulers confronted Peter and John about healing a man unable to walk. “Filled with the Holy Ghost,” Peter and John declared, with courage born of their faith, “If we this day be examined … by what means [this man] is made whole; be it known unto … all … that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom ye crucified, whom God raised from the dead, even by him doth this man stand here before you whole.”
As Peter and John of old, I too witness the reality of “Jesus Christ of Nazareth.” He lives. He guides this holy work, the restored gospel of Jesus Christ. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: James G. O. Fantone
title: Take Upon Us His Name
content:
My dear brothers and sisters, after my wife and I completed our service as mission leaders in the Philippines Antipolo Mission, our youngest daughter made a special request. She asked to complete her 11th grade through a home-school program.
My wife found an excellent school and asked me if I would stop by the registrar’s office and submit her remaining enrollment documents.
Upon arriving, I handed the paperwork to the registrar. She passed a document back, pointed to a line at the bottom, and asked me to write my daughter’s name and sign above it. However, my mind was preoccupied. I mistakenly thought she had instructed me to write my name.
With full confidence, I wrote “James Fantone” and signed. A few seconds later, I realized my error.
“Well,” I thought, “no big deal. This is an easy fix.” You see, our youngest daughter’s name is Amanda James Fantone. So I simply added “Amanda” right before my own name, and the error was quickly fixed.
Later, in a quiet moment of reflection, a profound question and a familiar scripture came to my mind. The question: What’s in a name? And the scripture, from King Benjamin: “There shall be no other name given nor any other way nor means whereby salvation can come unto the children of men, only in and through the name of Christ, the Lord Omnipotent” (Mosiah 3:17).
Pondering this, I began to see a significant spiritual contrast between my administrative quick fix and our Savior’s sacred invitation.
The Savior’s invitation is not merely for us to add His name to our name like a badge of religious affiliation. The Savior warned, “[Some] draw near to me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me” (Joseph Smith—History 1:19).
His invitation is for us to take upon us His name. It is an invitation to become more like Him through covenant keeping. The resurrected Lord asked, “Have they not read the scriptures, which say ye must take upon you the name of Christ, which is my name?” (3 Nephi 27:5; see also Mosiah 5:8; 6:2).
How do we, as covenant children of God, truly take upon ourselves the name of Jesus Christ? How does that manifest in our daily lives?
I love the simple yet profound answer taught by the prophet Moroni. He recorded that none were baptized “save they took upon them the name of Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end” (Moroni 6:3; see also Mosiah 18:13).
Taking upon us His name requires a lifelong determination to serve Him. And King Benjamin provided the divine key: “When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God” (Mosiah 2:17).
I was blessed to grow up in a home where serving others was taught through examples. We lived in a modest, three-bedroom bungalow—one room for me and my brother, one for our two older sisters, and one for our parents.
I distinctly remember a season when the boys’ room was not available for us to use. My mother, a public school teacher, learned that one of her recently graduated students could not pursue his vocational studies because his family could not afford housing near the school. Desiring to help him fulfill his potential, my parents opened our home and offered him the boys’ room.
During another season, it was the girls’ room that was occupied by someone else. When the Relief Society president in the ward spoke of a vulnerable family whose children desperately needed a safe place to stay, my parents, without hesitation, opened our doors, and some of the children indefinitely moved into our sisters’ room.
I believe with all my heart that if my parents had lived in Bethlehem when Joseph was searching for a place for Mary to give birth, and if by chance they knocked on our door, and if the boys’ and girls’ rooms were occupied, my parents would have gladly offered their room.
President Marion G. Romney taught this eternal truth: “Service is not something we endure on this earth so we can earn the right to live in the celestial kingdom. Service is the very fiber of which an exalted life in the celestial kingdom is made” (“The Celestial Nature of Self-Reliance,”, Mar. 2009, 19).
I witnessed this same courageous service in our remarkable full-time missionaries.
As a mission president, I held regular interviews. In their first few months, it was not uncommon for some to sit across from me in tears and say, “President, I am so sad, lonely, and homesick. The days feel so long and time is so slow; I don’t even know if I can last for three more months.” Yet these valiant missionaries got on their knees, put on their name tags, and went out to serve anyway.
A year later those exact same missionaries would sit in my office with glowing faces and say, “President, I am so happy! I love the people, and I love this work. But time is moving too fast—I don’t want this to end!”
Every time I witnessed this transformation, I marveled. “Did time actually change?”
You and I know the answer. Time did not change—the missionaries did.
The work did not change—the workers did.
Our missionaries changed.
When we genuinely take upon ourselves the name of Jesus Christ by losing ourselves in the service of others, something miraculous happens. We experience what Alma the Younger referred to as a “mighty change” in our hearts (Alma 5:14)—the kind of change that leads to true conversion and not merely personal elation. King Benjamin asked this penetrating question: “For how knoweth a man the master whom he has not served, and who is a stranger unto him, and is far from the thoughts and intents of his heart?” (Mosiah 5:13).
My beloved brothers and sisters, the Savior’s invitation is not for us to merely add His name to our names. His invitation is for us to take upon us His name by covenant and to serve Him with all our heart, might, mind, and strength—by lifting, loving, and serving our fellow men.
I stand before you today as a witness of His living reality. I have made a sacred covenant to take upon myself the name of Jesus Christ, and I am determined to strive to serve Him faithfully to the end.
I testify that He lives, that this is His restored Church, and that as we lose our lives in His service, we will find Him and we will find ourselves. In the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Edward Dube
title: Come unto Christ
content:
Thirty-nine years ago, President Dallin H. Oaks taught me about the character of Jesus Christ in a way I will never forget.
In 1987, I was a young missionary with only two years in the Church. At the mission office, a sign on the gate read, “Trespassers will be prosecuted.”
President Oaks asked that it be removed to avoid any impression of exclusion. Rather, we invite all to come unto Christ through faith in Him and His Atonement. In that moment, I gained the desire to love others as the Savior does. I love Him. I know He lives. He suffered for me in Gethsemane; “his sweat was as it were great drops of blood.” He suffered for me on the cross at Golgotha. I cannot comprehend that suffering, but I testify of His divinity.

President Oaks taught, “Jesus Christ did all of this because He loves all of the children of God.”
His suffering and atoning sacrifice show us how completely devoted He is to all of us. He invites us to come unto Him. Consider Moroni’s invitation: “Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, … deny yourselves of all ungodliness.”
Three key truths to note:

Come: It’s an action. We choose to move from our current place to a better place.

Deny yourselves: Surrender. Let go of the things that are holding us back.

Be perfected in Him: Come as we are with a willing heart. He will give us a new heart.

We do not need to perfect ourselves to come to Christ. We come to Christ to be perfected.
President Russell M. Nelson taught: “Perfection is pending. It can come in full only after the Resurrection and only through the Lord. It awaits all who love Him and keep His commandments.”
Last June on the way to the airport, President Brian Pace from the Wilmington North Carolina Stake asked, “Can we make one more ministering visit?”
“I have a flight to catch,” I thought. But he was already talking. “Brother Randall Child is a good man. He is trying very hard to stop smoking.”
There I am praying and panicking at the same time—I have never smoked a day in my life. What do I say? “Heavenly Father,” I pleaded, “please put words in my mouth.”
At the Childs’ home, following greetings and introductions, I empathized with his efforts to quit smoking. Then I asked, “Brother Child, how much do you love your wife, Laurin?”
His expression changed. “With all my heart.”
“Would you give up anything for her?” I asked.
My heart pounding, I extended the invitation: “Will you and Laurin go find a quiet room and choose a date to be sealed in the house of the Lord?”
A few minutes later they came back with an answer: “August 5.”
We left after kneeling in prayer. And just two months later they were sealed in the temple.

Sister Child shared this with me later: “I stayed awake all night because I couldn’t bear watching Randall suffer—wanting to be perfect in every way possible. So all night I cried and pleaded with the Lord to help him. In the early hours of the morning, the answer came very clear: ‘Randall doesn’t need to be perfect. He needs to do the very best he can.’”
