Randall added: “I had trust in the Lord. But when I heard Laurin praying for me—saying all I needed to do was the best I could—I knew then that she was an answer to my prayers.”
Brothers and sisters, let us consider Laurin’s answer to her prayer. The Lord said, “He needs to do the very best he can.” Randall didn’t perfect himself to come to Christ. He came to Christ—with prayer, with trust, and with a willing heart. The Savior, through His grace, helped him to let go of what was holding him back.
And that is why President Oaks had the sign on the gate taken down: “Trespassers will be prosecuted.” The adversary wants to hang that sign on the gate of our heart. Addiction, doubt, pride, pain, grief, guilt, materialism—or whatever is holding us back—he tells us this makes us unworthy to come unto Christ.
But Moroni taught it. Laurin heard it. Randall lived it. You too can live it. If you will “deny not his power, then are ye sanctified in Christ by the grace of God, through the shedding of the blood of Christ.”
One of our former missionaries wrote me recently and said, “As for my faith, my testimony is not as certain as it once was.”
To him, and to all who feel that same ache, I invite you, please come unto Christ and embrace His promise, “that [His] joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.”
My humble invitation to us all: Will you find one person and invite him or her to come unto Christ by exercising faith to follow His teachings, or invite a friend to meet with the missionaries?
As you lose yourself in helping him or her come unto Christ, you will find solutions to your current problems. Our Savior has promised, “For whosever will save his life shall lose it: and whosever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.” I testify of His divinity in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Quentin L. Cook
title: Integrity and Virtue Lead to Happiness
content:
Lifelong disciples of Jesus Christ best reflect the Savior’s teaching and direction when they joyfully live lives of integrity and virtue. The covenant path that will return us to our beloved Father in Heaven and His Son, Jesus Christ, is not obscure; it is well marked. We have been repeatedly taught the principles and covenants essential for this sacred path.
The virtuous, Christlike life necessary to sustain us and propel us along the covenant path has never been more important or challenging. If we are to be spiritually prepared to have the integrity and virtue required of disciples of Jesus Christ, we can stay on the path and continue to follow wise, righteous principles that lead to happiness.

Mary and I recently had the privilege of meeting with the missionaries in the Scotland/Ireland Mission. On the grounds of one building there is a replica of a message that significantly influenced President David O. McKay when he was a young missionary in Scotland.

As a new missionary, Elder McKay passed a building where the stone above the doorway bore this carved inscription: “WHAT-E’ER THOU ART ACT WELL THY PART.”

This message, “Whate’er thou art, act well thy part,” was so important and had such an impact on Elder McKay that he used it for inspiration as a missionary and for the rest of his life. He determined that whatever responsibility he had, he would do his very best.
When I was young, President McKay was the prophet, and his teachings had a lasting influence on me. I especially loved this message and have often referred to it.
It was clear that one of President McKay’s purposes in mentioning this incident was to teach that some conduct which is not inherently evil can keep us from engaging in spiritual matters that will bless us now and throughout eternity.
In our day, the application of this principle is essential if we are to be true lifelong disciples of Christ. We need to live our lives with integrity and follow His example. The Lord, speaking of one servant in Nauvoo, declared, “He may be trusted because of the integrity of his heart.” teaches, “Integrity includes being honest with God, yourself, your leaders, and others.”
President Spencer W. Kimball taught that “integrity (the willingness and ability to live by our beliefs and commitments) is one of the foundation stones of good character, and without good character one cannot hope to enjoy the presence of God here or in the eternities.”
In the Father’s plan, integrity, virtue, and happiness are intrinsically linked. Living a virtuous life with integrity aligns us with God’s will. True happiness, often translated as blessedness, is the actual outcome of integrity and being virtuous. Virtue includes not only a strong personal moral compass but also cleanliness, modesty, goodness, holiness, and reverence for the sacred.
The idea of happiness is a predominant goal of most people. The means of achieving the goal have been impacted in recent years by conduct and choices that do not result in happiness. A major concern is the lack of interest in the concept and pursuit of virtue. The relationship between virtue and happiness is not as well understood today as it was in the past.
In the United States we have been celebrating the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, which highlights the premise that all are created equal and are endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights and includes the inspiring emphasis on “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.” Some scholars have noted that the reference to “happiness” was understood by the founders to be based on living a virtuous life. Among the touching guidance that Joseph Smith received in Liberty Jail is the declaration, “Let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly.”
Significantly President McKay taught: “Happiness is the purpose and design of existence. ‘Men are that they might have joy’ [see 2 Nephi 2:25]. Virtue, uprightness, faithfulness, holiness, and keeping the commandments of God lead to a happy life.”
The Lord wants us to experience the joy of a virtuous life. He provides us with many beautiful gifts both physical and spiritual. Those who make sacrifices in His name will be richly rewarded.
In contrast, what we are seeing in society and social media today is conduct and language that are often coarse and crude and lack virtue. They are destructive of civil discourse. They also violate the basic principles the Savior taught. Any use of the internet to bully, destroy a reputation, or place a person in a bad light is reprehensible.
It is clear that evil communications are not just a matter of bad manners. If practiced by Latter-day Saints, they can adversely affect others who do not have a knowledge of God or a testimony of our Savior. The Lord has inspired marvelous technology that provides us with unparalleled experiences and opportunities when used wisely.
The Church has experienced physical and verbal attacks over the years. We cannot control the conduct of others, but we can strive to be a peaceable people who live in accordance with the Christlike conduct and virtues taught by our Savior, Jesus Christ. Both President Russell M. Nelson and President Dallin H. Oaks have been inspired to consistently talk about being righteous peacemakers.
If we dedicate some time every day to the scriptures and spiritual renewal, we will be deeply blessed. Young people who attend For the Strength of Youth and young single adult conferences often tell me the testimony meeting, a small portion of the event, is the most appreciated.
One of the special messages of the gospel of Jesus Christ teaches, “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” The Savior explained that He had not come to condemn the world but to save the world.
The Lord expects us to live lives of virtue and integrity and to follow His commandments. He taught, “And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” On another occasion, He said, “Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.”
The Apostle Paul beautifully taught, “Whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.”
We show our integrity by living virtuous lives and caring for and serving others. The ultimate reward of integrity and virtue is the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost. The Holy Ghost does not attend us when we do evil. But when we do what is right, He can dwell with us and guide us in all that we do.
Part of having integrity is acknowledging our faults to the Lord and repenting of transgressions. When we make repentance a constant, day-to-day part of our lives, we can approach the Lord with integrity and receive His saving blessings.
When I was a young missionary in the British Mission, one of my most memorable experiences was teaching a wonderful man who had served on a battleship in the European theater during World War II, 16 years before we met him. When we taught him the principles of repentance, he was overcome with emotion. He then shared with us the feelings he was experiencing while being taught, especially about repentance. He compared repentance to the feelings he had when he arrived back in England, departed from the battleship, and felt the earth of his island home under his feet. It had overwhelmed him, and he fell to his knees in appreciation.
When he learned that through repentance, baptism, and confirmation he could receive forgiveness for inappropriate conduct and sins he had engaged in, he was deeply touched. He said that his tender feelings about the Savior were spiritually profound. Just before his baptism, he prayed to the Lord to help him that he might be able to give other people the same joy that he was experiencing and then added, “Especially my family.”
Integrity, virtue, and ongoing repentance are the answer in a world where coarse language and serious challenges are so prevalent. I am eternally grateful for the Father’s plan of happiness. I testify that Jesus Christ accomplished the eternity-shaping sacrifice necessary for our salvation and exaltation, in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Alfred Kyungu
title: Using the Language of Peacemakers
content:
As the last speaker of the Sunday morning session of the April 2026 general conference, President Dallin H. Oaks said: “My brothers and sisters, as followers of Christ, let us follow Him by forgoing contention and by using the language and methods of peacemakers. In our families and other personal relationships, let us avoid what is harsh and hateful.”
As he concluded the conference on Sunday afternoon, President Oaks extended an invitation to all of us. He said, “As the messages from this conference are published, we invite all to study and ponder them prayerfully and to act in faith on the principles they explain.”
This invitation to forgo contention by using the language of peacemakers comes from the living prophet. It is not a simple suggestion; it is a call to discipleship as we follow Jesus Christ.
I began pondering on President Oaks’s invitation and how I could act with faith accordingly. It is a spiritual exercise to identify the language and expressions we need to forgo and then replace them with words and phrases that bring peace wherever we are and at all times.
From ancient times, the Lord has counseled His people to avoid contention, dispute, and language that create conflict. In Proverbs we read, “These six things doth the Lord hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him.” Among them are “a lying tongue, … a false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.”
During His earthly ministry, the Lord Jesus Christ taught:
“But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
“For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.”
The Apostle Paul wrote to the Ephesians, “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
Likewise, in Colossians the Saints were counseled to be wise even in their speech: “Let your speech be alway with grace, … that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
I believe that all of us in this mortal journey have been hurt by some form of humiliating, degrading, or discouraging language from a family member, a colleague at work, a friend, or even a fellow member of the Church.
There are expressions and words that can damage relationships and therefore need to be forgone in our communication. Examples include: “You are useless.” “You are stupid.” “You never do anything right.” “What is wrong with you?” “This is all your fault.” “You always mess things up.” “You never listen.” “You caused this problem.” “Leave me alone.” “I do not care.” “I do not need you in my life.” “I do not care about you.” “Just stop talking.” “I am tired of you.” The list could go on. Such words never edify. They weaken love, diminish respect, and damage relationships.
Rather than choosing words and language that escalate feelings of anger, disappointment, and frustration, let us use words that encourage understanding and peace. We must choose language that strengthens confidence and preserves relationships. Words such as: “Please.” “Thank you.” “I appreciate that.” “I respect your view.” “This is a good point.” “Let us slow down and talk.” “We can work this out.” “It is OK.” “Let us stay calm.” “We don’t have to rush.” “I care about you.” “I am here for you.” “You are not alone.” “How are you feeling?” “That matters to me.” “I’m sorry.” “Please forgive me.” “I forgive you.” “Let us start again.” “I don’t want this to divide us.”
As the converted Lamanites “buried the weapons of war, for peace,” we too can bury the language of contention for peace. President Thomas S. Monson taught us “to refrain from anger and to leave unsaid the harsh and hurtful things we may be tempted to say.” In hymn number 224, we sing, “I must speak the loving word, ere the sun goes down.” We learn from the New Testament that “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
Therefore, let us fill our hearts with the true doctrine of Christ, which has the power to change our language and help us speak more as peacemakers today, tomorrow, and always. As we follow Jesus Christ, we will not only feel His peace, but, as Elder Ulisses Soares said, “We can become instruments of His peace in the world.”
Let us repent for the harsh language and expressions that have offended our friends, leaders, family members, or colleagues. Let us pray for peaceful communication among us, regardless of the difference in our opinions. Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together. Let us speak with “warm respect when we speak with each other.” “Let us qualify for His blessings by using the language … of peacemakers.”
The Savior promised, “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you.” This peace is real. It is powerful, and it begins with us—with our hearts, our choices, and our words.
I bear my witness that our Heavenly Father loves us and desires us to live in peace and harmony. Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace. President Dallin H. Oaks is the prophet of God on the earth today, inviting us to communicate as peacemakers. In the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Ciro Schmeil
title: Consider Your Ways, and from This Day Will the Lord Bless You
content:
The Plan of Happiness

God is our Father in Heaven, and He prepared a plan for us to return to His presence. The scriptures call this the plan of salvation or “the great plan of happiness” (Alma 42:8). According to this plan, “this life is the time for [us] to prepare to meet God” (Alma 34:32).
And God did not leave us alone in this journey. As President Dallin H. Oaks has taught, God gave us “divine helps for mortality” that can help us back to His presence. I will mention two of these divine helps: the Savior Jesus Christ and our covenants.

Jesus Christ

Our Savior, Jesus Christ, and our covenants are essential to guide us through the covenant path and help us overcome our challenges and weaknesses. Jesus Christ knows us individually, and He will help us if we seek Him: “And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. … For if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them” (Ether 12:27).
According to this scripture, we need to be humble and have faith in Christ for the weak things to become strong. A central feature of humility is having a broken heart, which means to be receptive to the will of God. To be receptive to the will of God, we must have faith in Christ, which means that we trust Him even when we don’t have all the answers. President Oaks said: “By far, God’s strongest mortal help was His provision of a Savior, Jesus Christ, who would suffer to pay the price and provide forgiveness for repented sins. That merciful and glorious Atonement explains why faith in the Lord Jesus Christ is the first principle of the gospel.”

Covenants

We show our faith in Christ by making and keeping covenants with God. “A covenant is a sacred promise between God and His children. God gives the conditions for the covenant, and His children agree to obey those conditions. God promises to bless His children as they fulfill the covenant.”
Covenants bind us to Jesus Christ because He is central to every covenant we make. In Matthew 11, the Savior extends a beautiful invitation and a promise to all of us. He said:
“Come unto me, … and I will give you rest.
“Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; … and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
“For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).
It is through covenants that we become yoked with the Savior Jesus Christ and our burdens become lighter.
The baptismal covenant is the first covenant we make with God. We then make a new covenant with Him each week as we partake of the sacrament during our Sunday worship wherein we renew promises made at baptism and covenant to always remember the Savior. Jesus Christ instituted the sacrament to help us remember Him with the promise that if we do so, we will have His Spirit with us (see Luke 22:19–20; 3 Nephi 18:11).
In the sacrament prayer we have a good reminder that we do not need to be perfect to partake of the sacrament. We need to be willing to take upon us His name, remember Him, and keep His commandments, and in return we have the promise to always have His Spirit with us. The sacrament is essential to have the Spirit and the strength to continue on the covenant path.
Elder Dale G. Renlund has reminded and warned us that “the time will come, in each of your lives, when there will be a hesitation to go to church and partake of the sacrament. If it hasn’t happened yet, it will. But know this: if you follow the Savior’s direction and go and partake of the sacrament, with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, blessings will pour upon you that will keep you firm, that will keep you solid, that will keep you established on that firm foundation that is Jesus Christ.”
In we also learn that “as we make our Sabbath activities compatible with God’s intent for the day, we will feel joy and peace. We will be spiritually nourished and physically refreshed.” What a blessing it is for us to partake of the sacrament each week.
The sacrament also prepares us to make and keep temple covenants. We can draw insight about the importance and the blessings of the temple covenants as we read the account of the prophet Haggai in the Old Testament.
The Lord had commanded the Israelites to rebuild the temple, but they did not make it a priority. Displeased with them, the Lord said:
“Consider your ways.
“Ye have sown much, and bring in little; … and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.
“Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Consider your ways.
“… Why? … Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house” (Haggai 1:5–7, 9).
We learn from this account that the Lord could not magnify their efforts because their actions were not aligned with God’s will. Although they were doing much, they were not accomplishing much because God’s holy house was not a priority in their lives.
As they considered their ways, they repented and followed God’s direction. As soon as they started to rebuild the temple, the Lord said, “From this day will I bless you” (Haggai 2:19).

Blessings

May we also consider our ways. Heavenly Father is not asking us to physically build the temple, but He is asking us to build a strong relationship with Him and His Son, Jesus Christ, through our covenants. He will magnify our efforts as we consider our ways and make the proper adjustments to make and keep covenants with Him. God knows what is best for us and is eager to bless us. Remember what He said to the Israelites: “From this day will I bless you” (Haggai 2:19). I know that God keeps His promises. I have seen it in my life. He gave me spiritual and physical strength when I needed it most.
The sacrament has helped me to keep my baptismal and temple covenants. It is a weekly reminder of what the Savior Jesus Christ has done for me and how much I need Him in my life as I walk the covenant path back to His presence.
May we consider our ways and remember the words of King Benjamin when he said: “Consider on the blessed and happy state of those that keep the commandments of God. For behold, they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual; and if they hold out faithful to the end they are received into heaven, that thereby they may dwell with God in a state of never-ending happiness” (Mosiah 2:41). This is possible only as we make and keep covenants. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
title: The Gospel of Jesus Christ Is for All
content:
This is the Church of Jesus Christ, so named because it is His Church with the restored fulness of His doctrine and authority in these latter days.
It is “His Church” for many reasons. As we state in our first article of faith, “We believe in God, the Eternal Father, and in His Son, Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Ghost.” God the Father, the great Elohim, is the Father of our spirits, the framer of heaven and earth, and the author of the plan of our salvation. Jesus Christ is His Only Begotten Son, Jehovah, and the Messiah, “the God of the whole earth.” As the Book of Mormon declares, “Salvation was, and is, and is to come, in and through the atoning blood of Christ, the Lord Omnipotent.”
Latter-day Saints invite each other and all men and women everywhere to “come unto Christ.” As a prophet has told us in the Book of Mormon, “I would that ye should come unto Christ, who is the Holy One of Israel, and partake of his salvation, and the power of his redemption.”
As your President, I pray for what our Heavenly Father wants for each of us—to be active members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, proceeding forward on the covenant path into the eternities. We need one another’s prayers. I feel the positive effect of your prayers. I am thankful, and I love you.
We all have present or future concerns or struggles we are trying to overcome. Those may include questions or doubts. Whatever they are, the way to overcome them is to get closer to our Savior, Jesus Christ. Again and again, He has taught us that He is the way. Focus on developing your faith in God and the mission of His Son, Jesus Christ. Strong faith requires more than strong desire. It means daily trying, one step at a time, with prayer and scriptural learning.
We are all a work in progress. We are all at different places on what President Russell M. Nelson called “the covenant path.” We need to be patient with one another and, occasionally, even with ourselves. Overcoming uncertainty and doubt—which may include resolving conflicts between the evolving understanding of science and the sometimes incomplete teachings of religion—can be a lengthy process. It involves building faith and strengthening humility. Hold on to the first article of faith even if something else is uncertain. And while you wait, wait upon the Lord, which includes trusting in His timing as well as in His promises.
A major source of concern to your prophet leaders are those members of diminishing faith in Jesus Christ. We love you, young and old, men and women. So does the Lord God! He is relentless in His loving pursuit of each of you. Because of this concern and according to His words, I urge you to keep the commandments and be true to the covenants so many of you have made to guide you along the covenant path. Never let your secular learning limit your spiritual horizons.
We are grateful to know that there are two methods of gaining needed knowledge: (1) the evolving disclosures of man through the scientific method and digital information, which may be inaccurate, and (2) the truths discovered through the spiritual method, which begins with faith in God and relies on scriptures, inspired teaching, and personal revelation. There is no ultimate conflict between knowledge obtained by these different methods because God, our omnipotent Eternal Father, knows all truth and expects us to learn by both methods.
Along the way we should work to draw closer to Jesus Christ by increasing our humility. President Spencer W. Kimball defined humility as “teachableness.” He explained: “Teachableness [is] an ability to realize that all virtues and abilities are not concentrated in one’s self. … [Humility] is forgiving others in the realization that there may be errors of the same kind or worse [that we ourselves commit].”
Protect yourself with the weekly renewing of your covenants by partaking of the sacrament and with consistent efforts to live according to those sacred covenants. Those who have been endowed should include regular attendance at the temple. These simple practices will protect and strengthen you.
The Book of Mormon teaches that the great Creator died “for all men, that all men might become subject unto him.” This means that if our sins are to be forgiven through His Atonement, we must comply with the conditions He has prescribed, including faith, repentance, and baptism. The fulfillment of these conditions depends on our desires, our choices, and our actions. “He cometh into the world that he may save all men if they will hearken unto his voice.”
The Book of Mormon adds to our knowledge of how our Savior’s earthly ministry reached out to all of His scattered flock. It records His appearance and teachings to the Nephites on the American continent. There He repeated that the Father had commanded Him to visit the other sheep which were not of the land of Jerusalem. The Savior also taught that He would visit others “who [had] not as yet heard [His] voice,” such as the “lost tribes of Israel.”
The Book of Mormon is a great witness that the Lord loves all people and reaches out to all, everywhere.
“Know ye not that I, the Lord your God, have created all men, and that I remember those who are upon the isles of the sea; and that I rule in the heavens above and in the earth beneath; and I bring forth my word unto the children of men, yea, even upon all the nations of the earth?”
Other Book of Mormon teachings contradict the erroneous assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. The Book of Mormon teaches that our Savior inviteth “all to come unto him … ; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile.” His grace is for all. Similarly, the Book of Mormon tells us that the children of God in “every nation” have His promise that He “manifesteth himself unto all those who believe in him, by the power of the Holy Ghost.”
These promises from the Book of Mormon are true. Millions believe them and have had experiences to affirm their truth. I invite all to believe them.
We believe that the Lord will eventually cause the inspired teachings He has given to His children in various nations to be brought forth for the benefit of all people. This will include accounts of the visit of the resurrected Lord to what we call the lost tribes of Israel and His revelations to all the seed of Abraham.
We live in the day foretold when righteousness is sent forth out of heaven and truth out of the earth “to sweep the earth as with a flood, [and] to gather out [the] elect from the four quarters of the earth.” All around us we see evidence that many in the world are hungry for our Savior, Jesus Christ, and His teachings. As declared on its title page, the Book of Mormon has come forth that we “may know [of] the covenants of the Lord” and also for the convincing of all “that Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God, manifesting himself unto all nations.” I call upon all to act on these truths and to share them with others that we may all draw closer to Jesus Christ, our Savior. I make this invitation and add my testimony of Him and His mission in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Dieter F. Uchtdorf
title: Christ-Centered Unity
content:
It is such a joy to be with you today.
Recently, Sister Uchtdorf and I attended the baptisms of two of our great-grandchildren. We rejoiced with them as they chose to follow Jesus Christ and made sacred covenants to take upon themselves the Savior’s name, keep God’s commandments, and serve Him. By entering the waters of baptism, they literally followed not only the Savior’s example but also the examples of siblings, cousins, parents, and many trusted friends.
My heart fills with gratitude when I think back on my own baptism. I was baptized at age eight in an impressive indoor public swimming pool. Back then, as we walked into the water, my mind and heart were preoccupied with this thought: “The pool is getting deeper and deeper, and I can’t swim!”
Spiritual growth is rarely dramatic at the beginning. Like an exponential curve, it often starts gradually—with loving parents, simple prayers, and small acts of faith.
Then, as we progress along the covenant path, our relationship with God deepens, and our capacity for a joyful life expands. The temple endowment, missionary service, celestial marriage in the house of the Lord, ongoing service in God’s kingdom—these experiences do not merely add to our discipleship; they multiply greatly our potential for divine understanding and blessings. The arc of discipleship helps us to grow closer to our role model, Jesus Christ, and it continues eternally.
Baptism is the gate through which we enter this “strait and narrow path.” We must enter that gate one by one. Baptism is an individual ordinance.
However, it is also a unifying one. It joins us to a worldwide community of Saints.
Through baptism, we become not only covenant individuals but also part of a covenant people.
When we are baptized, we declare before God and witnesses that we “are desirous to come into the fold of God.” We show that we do not want to live only for ourselves. We desire to be part of a people who “bear one another’s burdens,” “mourn with those that mourn,” and “comfort those that stand in need of comfort.”
In other words, when we join the Church of Jesus Christ, we say—humbly, gratefully, and with quiet confidence—that we want to follow our beloved Savior, Jesus Christ. And we want to walk that path together.

Jesus Christ Unites Us

When I read the scriptures, I’m impressed with how much of the Savior’s work has to do with bringing people peacefully together. For example, think about the world Jesus Christ was born in. At that time and place, Jews and Samaritans avoided each other. Gentiles were considered unclean. Pharisees and Sadducees agreed on little except their dislike of publicans and sinners. The people were divided in a dozen different ways—culturally, politically, religiously.
When you think about it, it wasn’t so different from our world today.
But the Savior of the world, the Son of God, transcended worldly boundaries and divisions. As Paul said, He “[broke] down the middle wall of partition between us.” He consistently reached out to those who would otherwise be shunned as outsiders. He touched lepers. He praised Gentiles for their faith. He used a Samaritan as an example of compassion. He gathered people from different walks of life and asked them to serve together in positions of trust. He ministered to the poor and rich alike. And today He continues to invite all to come unto Him.
However, while Jesus Christ is reaching across worldly boundaries to unite Heavenly Father’s family, Satan is seeking to divide us. He aims to weaken God’s children by isolating us from each other. He emphasizes our differences, making them feel like impassable barriers. We can see the fruits of his efforts in the contention, mistrust, and hatred all around us.
And yet the Savior’s work of gathering continues, undaunted. In fact, it is accelerating. And as covenant followers of Jesus Christ, we recognize that we are all brothers and sisters, joyfully participating with Christ in gathering and uniting the great family of God.

The Unity Jesus Christ Offers

Throughout history, people have united over a variety of purposes. Some have united over social causes or political ideas. Some unite to celebrate their cultural heritage. Some, sadly, have united because of hatred for another group. Others unite around hobbies, professional interests, or even love for a favorite soccer team or brand of soft drink. Often these desires to unify are driven by very strong feelings or opinions.
In the Savior’s Church, it is not our political views, culture, or personal interests that unite us. It is our love for God and neighbor, God’s children. It is our commitment to our covenants with Jesus Christ and to His restored gospel. We are “one in Christ.”
The Book of Mormon tells us of two nations, the Nephites and the Lamanites, who were engaged in one of the longest-running sibling rivalries in the world. Wars and contentions literally defined their history for generations. But all of that changed when Jesus Christ appeared, taught them His gospel, and established His Church. For the next 200 years, the love of God replaced contention, and bitter enemies became “one”—they became “the children of Christ.” They became His covenant people.
The catalyst for this change was Jesus Christ and His doctrine.
It always has been, and it always will be.
Jesus Christ has the power to change us—you and me—purify us, and unite us. The closer we come to Him, the closer we will come to each other—and the closer we will come to the unity He wants for us.
If we are not one, we are not His.
When our attention is riveted on Christ, superficial things are hardly worth noticing. We learn to see as He sees—looking on the heart rather than the outward appearance. When our “eye [is] single to [His] glory,” we are “filled with [His] light.” When we try to be a little more patient, a little kinder, more forgiving, more helpful, more neighborly, there will be less room for pride or judgmental attitudes or contention. Such things can no longer stand in the way of Christ-centered unity with each other and with our beloved Father in Heaven.
Does that sound too lofty? Out of reach? It may seem that way. But then, the Savior is always urging us to reach beyond what seems possible, because “with God all things are possible.”
We may not achieve perfect Christ-centered unity in this life, but the “spiritual momentum” we build here will carry us into eternity. In other words, now is the time to unify. Unity won’t magically happen in the next life if we haven’t earnestly tried to learn it here. Every step we take toward unity matters, however small it may seem.

The Unifying Power of the Sacrament

On this path to more unity, let us not miss the unifying power of the sacrament. Each week we gather as fellow disciples of Jesus Christ to renew our baptismal covenant and to remember all the covenants we’ve personally made with God. My dear brothers and sisters, the sacrament can become a fresh starting point for our personal relationship with God and for a greater Christ-centered unity in our lives.
Have you ever noticed that the sacrament is the only ordinance we receive during which we are not addressed by name? Rather, it is performed for “the souls of all those who partake of it.” The only names that are used are those of God the Father and Jesus Christ. We partake individually but also as a group.
There is something powerful, something empowering, about renewing covenants with God while surrounded by brothers and sisters who have made or are considering making the same covenants. The sacrament is a weekly reminder, a sacred reminder, that we are not alone. We have the Savior, and we have each other.

Blessings of Unity in Christ

Wherever you are, I invite you to join the Christ-centered unity we are trying to build. It would be incomplete without you. Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.
Jesus promised, “Where two or three are gathered … in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” I testify that the more united in Christ we are and the more we desire to build bridges instead of walls, the more our individual lives, our families, our communities, and our nations will experience God’s presence and supernal blessings.
May God bless us to unite in the Savior’s name and center our minds, hearts, and lives on Him. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Andrea Muñoz Spannaus
title: God Is at Your Side
content:
Dear young women, how crucial and important you are as members of the Church of Jesus Christ in these latter days!
When I was your age, I remember a lesson where we studied the thirteenth article of faith. When the class was over, I kept thinking about this part: “If there is anything virtuous, lovely, or of good report or praiseworthy, we seek after these things.” I wondered what my aspirations were and what I wanted to achieve in my life. So I decided to make a list of those things—good, positive things that would bring me closer to God and would help me learn, contribute, create, and be happy. I spent that Sunday afternoon thinking and writing about the virtuous and good things I wanted to have happen in my life.
Today I invite you to look at your life and what you want to achieve with enthusiasm and the certainty that your Father in Heaven will guide you on that journey and show you the best way to make the righteous desires of your heart come true.
I want to illustrate this concept with an experience. On my way to the dentist, I put the address in my phone. While I was driving on the freeway, the GPS thought I was on a parallel street and kept telling me to turn right—when there was no place to turn. Finally, I pulled off the freeway and called my husband for help. When I gave him my exact location, he was able to guide me to the place I wanted to go.
Dear young women, the Lord knows where you are; He has your exact location and can guide you. He knows your dreams and your gifts. He knows when you feel alone and what your questions are. He knows your challenges and how to turn your weaknesses into strengths. He knows everything. And knowing everything about you does not make Him love you less.
Once a young man came running, kneeling before Jesus Christ, and asking Him, “What can I do to gain eternal life?” The young man said he had always obeyed the commandments. Would Jesus know what else this young man could do? Of course! But before He tells him, look at what happened. In Mark 10:21, we read, “Jesus beholding him loved him.”
Can you imagine those moments when Jesus looks at this young man? A look that conveys only love: love of the highest quality. Only after transmitting that love did He tell him what he could do to improve.
Our Father and our Savior know you and have the same perfect love for you. Part of that love and mercy is giving us many opportunities and being patient as we learn and work on our list of aspirations.
Dear young women, I testify that you are beloved daughters of heavenly parents, with a divine nature and an eternal destiny. Each of you has a crucial and important work to do here on earth. That work is different for each person, but if you choose to love God and Jesus Christ and to trust Them, doing that work will bring you the same great joy.
I would like to share seven ways that will help you in this endeavor. I invite you to listen to the Spirit to choose one to focus on over the next few weeks.

Partake of the sacrament with a humble heart, grateful for the promise that as you keep your covenants, the Holy Ghost will be your constant companion. Begin each day by asking the Father for that companionship.

Repent daily and at the end of the day, as you pray, ask for forgiveness.

Study the scriptures with a desire to know God’s character so you can do His will, increase your love for Him, and advance His work.

Study what it means to have ministering angels help you.

Protect your sleep; go to bed early. Get enough sleep to keep your mind clear and alert. When we sleep, the brain performs vital functions to work properly.

Limit cell phone use. Social media makes us believe we are connected; however, it is a thief of our peace of mind, self-esteem, and the real connection that makes us feel loved, accepted, heard, and valued when spending time face to face with others.

And number seven is an invitation from our prophet, President Dallin H. Oaks: “Seek friends … who are striving to follow the Lord … with whom you can feel the Spirit and … reinforce your faith.”

A few years ago, we had recently moved from Argentina to the United States, and I was learning English. (I am still learning!) At that time, my calling involved teaching. That day I felt everything I said had been wrong, that I had mispronounced words and made many grammatical errors—that it had been a complete disaster! I felt depressed, as if I were in a black cloud. I wondered why God had given me this calling if I couldn’t even speak! I was confused and didn’t see a way out. That night I went to sleep in tears, hoping I would feel better in the morning. But in the morning, I woke up feeling the same.
Then my husband gave me a priesthood blessing, and in that moment, I felt the heavens open. In the blessing, I was told, “Satan wants to destroy your self-esteem, your mind, your thoughts, and your spirit.” And then I received these words: “But the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost are at your side.”
Dear young women, I testify that the Lord has greater power than the enemy. He knows where you are and has promised to lead you by the hand. Always put Him first and remain faithful to the covenants you made at your baptism. Angels can minister to you. The Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost are at your side.
I invite you to study the thirteenth article of faith and to create your own list of aspirations. I express my love for you and my confidence in all the beautiful things you will achieve in your lives. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Moisés Villanueva
title: “Prove Me Now Herewith”
content:
When I was 10 years old, my family and I were baptized as members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Entering the covenant path brought some profound changes to our lives. I had never attended any church before. I now understand that those changes reflected our sincere efforts to apply the doctrine of Jesus Christ in our lives.
Perhaps the change that required the greatest faith and sacrifice was to honorably pay a full tithe.
Those were difficult years financially. My mother had separated from my father and worked tirelessly to provide for our family. Supporting eight children—most of us still very young—was no easy task. Yet when the missionaries taught us the law of tithing, my mother chose to trust the Lord’s promise as recorded by Malachi: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Malachi 3:10).
The Lord taught this important principle:
“There is a law, irrevocably decreed in heaven before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated—
“And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated” (Doctrine and Covenants 130:20–21).
I bear witness to this great truth.
As the Lord declared, “Who am I, saith the Lord, that have promised and have not fulfilled?” (Doctrine and Covenants 58:31).
Sometimes we expect the Lord’s blessings to come the way we would wish, rather than in His own way and timing.
After a sacrament meeting, a faithful sister shared that her testimony of the law of tithing had begun to weaken. She explained that although she had always paid a full tithe, she had never received the job promotion she had hoped for nor even the salary increase she deserved.
The counsel I gave her is the same counsel I share with you today.
In his address “The Windows of Heaven,” Elder David A. Bednar taught, “As we live the law of tithing, we often receive significant but subtle blessings that are not always what we expect and easily can be overlooked” (, Nov. 2013, 17).
Elder Bednar’s words prompted me to make a list of the blessings I have received through faithfully paying my tithing. The Holy Ghost helped me recognize many blessings:

I have enjoyed steady employment for many years.

My wife, my children, and I have been blessed with good health.

Our home and temporal possessions have been preserved, even during difficult times.

The Lord has blessed me with the ability to manage my time and resources so I could obtain an education.

I have developed the gift of gratitude by learning to appreciate the Lord’s hand in each of His tender mercies.

I have learned to recognize the influence of the Holy Ghost when making important decisions in my life.

These blessings, both temporal and spiritual—and many others—are evidence that the Lord has indeed opened the windows of heaven and poured out His promised blessings in abundance. I invited that sister to write her own list of the significant yet subtle blessings the Lord had given her—blessings that are often easy to overlook.
Later I heard another faithful sister share in a sacrament meeting that the 20-liter (5-gallon) propane tank in her home had lasted far longer than she had expected. It almost seemed as though it would never run out. She knew this was one of the Lord’s tender mercies for paying an honorable tithing.
I was reminded of the Lord’s words to the children of Israel: “And I have led you forty years in the wilderness: your clothes are not waxen old upon you, and thy shoe is not waxen old upon thy foot” (Deuteronomy 29:5).
Have you ever asked yourselves whether the Lord has caused your personal possessions to last longer because you have faithfully lived the law of tithing?
I have seen those subtle blessings many times in my own life.
When I think of my mother’s faith during those difficult years, I also think of the widow of Zarephath.
The Lord told Elijah, “Arise, get thee to Zarephath … : behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee” (1 Kings 17:9).
Elijah found the widow gathering sticks. He asked her for some water and for a morsel of bread. She explained that she had only a handful of meal and a little oil—enough to prepare one final meal for herself and her son and then die.
Elijah then said, “Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son” (1 Kings 17:13).
He promised that her barrel of meal would not be exhausted and her cruse of oil would not fail until the Lord sent rain upon the earth.
She “did according to the saying of Elijah” (1 Kings 17:15).
Elijah understood that blessings will come after the trial of our faith. The widow trusted in Elijah’s words and offered up all that she had (see also Mark 12:41–44).
Then the Lord’s promise was fulfilled: “And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by Elijah” (1 Kings 17:16).
I am especially grateful that my mother trusted the Lord’s promises and chose to live the law of tithing regardless of our difficult circumstances.
I bear my testimony that God is our loving Heavenly Father. He knows each of us and is aware of our needs even before we ask (see Matthew 6:8). I testify that Jesus Christ is the Son of the living God and that He directs His Church today. He gives us commandments because He wants us to receive His blessings.
When we live the law of tithing, the Lord indeed opens the windows of heaven and pours out His promised blessings “that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Malachi 3:10). I so testify in the sacred name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: David A. Bednar
title: Sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise
content:
I learned a vital lesson many years ago from President Boyd K. Packer. He said:
“No matter what citizenship or race, whether male or female, no matter what occupation, no matter your education, regardless of the generation in which one lives, life is a homeward journey for all of us, back to the presence of God.
“Ordinances and covenants become our credentials for admission into His presence. To worthily receive them is the quest of a lifetime; to keep them thereafter is the challenge of mortality.”
I pray the Holy Ghost will instruct and enlighten each of us as we consider the importance of ordinances and covenants as spiritual credentials for our journey home to Heavenly Father.

The Parable of the Passport

I begin with a short story. Once a man wanted to visit family members in a distant country. He planned his trip, packed his suitcase, and traveled by airplane to the city where his relatives lived.
The man excitedly exited the airplane and walked to the passport control checkpoint. He had a valid passport issued by an authorized agency of his country’s government. He presented his passport to a border official, who verified the man’s identity, nationality, and reasons for visiting the country. But the man had not taken good care of his passport. The personal information page had been stained and damaged. And a ripped page had been repaired in an unauthorized manner with tape and glue.
Consequently, the border official rejected his passport and refused to provide the stamp necessary for him to enter the country. The man was disappointed and perplexed about what he should do next.
The lesson of this story is quite simple: the integrity of a passport must be maintained over time. Holding a valid passport provided the opportunity for the man to enter the country, but the passport alone did not guarantee he actually would be allowed to enter the country.
Of course, this simple analogy has limitations. Unlike damage to a physical passport, the adversities and afflictions we experience through no fault of our own do not diminish God’s promises to us or invalidate our covenants.

Covenants, Ordinances, and Promised Blessings

For disciples of Jesus Christ, receiving priesthood ordinances and entering into sacred covenants are essential steps in the “quest of a lifetime” to align our hearts, minds, and lives with God’s will.
A covenant is a solemn promise—an enduring commitment between God and His sons and daughters. God establishes the conditions of all gospel covenants, and His children exercise their moral agency to learn about and consent to what He asks them to do.
Covenants are received through sacred ordinances. An ordinance is a holy act performed by the authority of the priesthood that has spiritual purpose and eternal significance and is related to God’s laws and statutes. Ordinances also teach us about the nature of the covenants we accept in our lives.
The covenants and ordinances of the Savior’s restored gospel are spiritual credentials that can open wide the heavenly windows of opportunity to receive in our lives divine purpose, direction, and strength. God promises His sons and daughters supernal blessings for honoring covenants, including obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel of Jesus Christ. Ongoing faithfulness is required for those credentials to be valid and for promised blessings to be received.

The Holy Ghost Is the Holy Spirit of Promise

The Holy Ghost is the third member of the Godhead. He is a personage of spirit, testifies of all truth, and is the witness of and messenger for the Father and the Son.
The Holy Ghost is also described in scripture as the Holy Spirit of Promise, who ratifies or confirms as acceptable to God the righteous acts of His children. Ultimately, all gospel ordinances and covenants must be sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise. As the Lord revealed to the Prophet Joseph Smith, “All covenants … not made and entered into and sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise … are of no efficacy, virtue, or force in and after the resurrection from the dead.”
When sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise, an ordinance, vow, or covenant is binding on earth and in heaven. This sealing is conditional in mortality and can be broken or forfeited through unrighteousness.
Receiving this ratifying sealing by the Holy Ghost typically is not a one-time event; rather, it comes over time as we repent sincerely and consistently, honor our covenants, and yield our hearts unto God. Righteously seeking for this blessing is “the challenge of mortality,” as described by President Packer.
Just as the man in my passport story needed an authorized stamp in his passport to enter a foreign country, so each of us needs the verifying witness of the Holy Spirit of Promise in order for us to receive the eternal blessings associated with the covenants and ordinances of the Savior’s gospel.
Each of us should ever be grateful for sacred opportunities to “walk in all the ordinances of the Lord” and to receive by the Holy Spirit of Promise, “in process of time,” the ratifying seal that guarantees all promised blessings.

The Sealing Ordinance

The sealing of a man and a woman in the house of the Lord is a crowning covenant and ordinance of the Savior’s restored gospel. And importantly, understanding the doctrinal importance of a sealing ordinance being sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise helps to address, in part, deeply personal questions about whether another person’s choices can deprive a faithful covenant keeper of eternal blessings.
The sealing ordinance includes two fundamental and related parts: (1) the eternal union of a man and a woman in marriage—what may be understood as a lateral sealing—and (2) the sealing of the husband and wife into God’s eternal family and the linking of humankind through all generations—what may be understood as a vertical sealing. Both elements of the ordinance are vital.
The intended and prayed-for outcomes of a temple sealing between a man and a woman include a lifetime of spiritual growth, marital devotion, fidelity, working together to overcome the uncertainties and challenges of mortality, and enduring happiness.
Sometimes, unfortunately, the intended and prayed-for outcomes do not happen. A spouse’s sins, infidelity, personal apostasy, or other difficulties may cause contention, alienation, and even divorce. In these cases, a faithful spouse may ask, “Can the unrighteous exercise of moral agency by another person rob me of what God has promised?” The answer to this question is an emphatic no!
The unworthy actions of a spouse certainly bring heartache and sorrow to the other spouse and family members. However, unrighteousness by one person cannot hinder or thwart the flow of God’s love, strength, and blessings to another person. The power of the Lord’s infinite and eternal Atonement can overcome all things, all the time, everywhere, for every person who holds fast to their covenants with Him.
A spouse who violates covenants and does not repent relinquishes the opportunity to receive for himself or herself the ratifying seal of the Holy Spirit of Promise for both the lateral and vertical aspects of the sealing ordinance.
A faithful spouse who honors covenants and presses forward in faith remains worthy to receive for himself or herself the ratifying seal of the Holy Spirit of Promise for the vertical aspect of the sealing ordinance and to receive all other associated individual blessings.
You may ask, “How can this be the case if a temple marriage does not endure?”
The revealed doctrine of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints does not address all details of and nuances about such cases. I do not know and cannot explain precisely how and when promised blessings are received. But I do know promised blessings will be received. No faithful disciple will ultimately be deprived of any eternal blessing God has promised because of another individual’s unrighteous exercise of moral agency.
I conclude with the reassuring testimony of King Benjamin: “I would desire that ye should consider on the blessed and happy state of those that keep the commandments of God. For behold, they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual; and if they hold out faithful to the end they are received into heaven, that thereby they may dwell with God in a state of never-ending happiness. O remember, remember that these things are true; for the Lord God hath spoken it.”
I joyfully testify to the truthfulness of King Benjamin’s prophetic promise in the sacred name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Thabo Lebethoa
title: Jesus Christ Is the Light and Life of the World
content:
In my home country of South Africa, it is customary for parents to give their children names with special meaning. My name is Thabo. It means “joy.” My beloved wife’s middle name is Gadifele. It means “eternal or endless.” Put together, our names mean “eternal joy.” What an expectation!
But shortly after we were married, a discussion one evening unexpectedly turned into our first serious disagreement. It quickly escalated into an argument, and we went from being a cheerful, happy couple to giving each other the silent treatment in a selfish state of quiet desperation.
Many of us have experienced such moments when a conversation or discussion with a spouse, a child, a family member, a friend, a colleague, or a neighbor did not end as we hoped. In such moments, what may have begun as a simple exchange may leave us with feelings of anger, disappointment, frustration, or even regret.
Whilst I was pondering about what to do, the words Jesus Christ spoke when He appeared to the people of Nephi in the Book of Mormon came to mind. He taught:
“For verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me, but is of the devil, who is the father of contention, and he stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger, one with another.
“Behold, this is not my doctrine, to stir up the hearts of men with anger, one against another; but this is my doctrine, that such things should be done away” (3 Nephi 11:29–30; emphasis added).

Jesus Christ Is the Light and Life of the World

These words from the scriptures enlightened my mind and helped me know how to resolve the challenge I was facing. This enlightenment comes from the Savior. In 3 Nephi 11:11, the Savior said, “I am the light and the life of the world” (emphasis added). Through His Spirit, He enlightens our minds (see Doctrine and Covenants 6:15). His light is also revealed through His perfect life and teachings. He declared, “I am the light; I have set an example for you” (3 Nephi 18:16), and His words are “a light unto [our] path” (Psalm 119:105).

How Can We Receive More of the Savior’s Light in Our Lives?

Many of us may wonder how we can receive more of the Savior’s light as we navigate through the daily challenges and struggles in our lives. We may be concerned about becoming self-reliant; meeting the demands placed upon us at school or at work; feeling inadequacy, fear, and doubt; dealing with the loss of a loved one; or simply knowing what to do with our lives. Whatever concerns, challenges, and struggles we may have in our lives, the answer is always Jesus Christ.
Jesus Christ can bring light in our moments of darkness and restore hope where there is hopelessness. He knows where we have been, where we are, and where we need to be. Through Him, today can be a new day and tomorrow can be a better day.
Here are some things we can do to increase the Savior’s light in our lives.

First, Increase Our Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ

Having faith in Jesus Christ means trusting that He understands our daily difficulties and knows how to help us rise above them because He has experienced all our pains, afflictions, and infirmities (see Alma 7:11–12). We need to trust that He is always ready to help us as we remember to “look unto [Him] in every thought” and “doubt not, fear not” (Doctrine and Covenants 6:36).
In the October 2024 general conference, President Dieter F. Uchtdorf taught: “Strong faith in Jesus Christ doesn’t happen overnight. No, in this mortal world, it’s the thorns and thistles of doubt that grow spontaneously. The healthy, fruitful tree of faith requires intentional effort” (“Nourish the Roots, and the Branches Will Grow,”, Nov. 2024, 102).
President Dallin H. Oaks in an address to BYU students taught that “strong faith requires more than strong desire. It means daily trying, one step at a time, with prayer and scripture study” (“Coming Closer to Jesus Christ” [Brigham Young University devotional, Feb. 10, 2026], 2, speeches.byu.edu).

Second, Study the Scriptures Daily, Especially the Book of Mormon

In, we learn, “As people read and pray about the Book of Mormon, they will come to know the Savior better and experience His love” ( [2023], 115).
There is no single right way to study the scriptures. We may choose to read chronologically, study by topic, focus on a particular question, or begin with a passage or verse that draws our attention. We may also choose a time that best fits our circumstances. Ultimately, the method, timing, and length of our scripture study matter less than the consistency and sincerity of our effort.
Whilst we were serving as mission leaders in our home country, one of our missionaries shared a story of a man they were teaching who, after reading the Book of Mormon, took a shovel, dug a hole in his garden, emptied a newly purchased large tin of coffee into it, and buried it. The man was enlightened by the Spirit on the changes he needed to make and acted upon it. We too can receive enlightenment as we study our scriptures.

Third, Practice Repentance Daily

Repentance means a change of mind and a turning of the heart to God. Let us ponder about the changes that we need to make in our lives, and these may include how we use our time, the things we watch or listen to, and the language and tone we use as we communicate with others. Perhaps we can begin by asking ourselves what is it that we need to change in our lives. It is important to remember that we do not need to go through this alone. The Savior is always ready to help because He sees the end from the beginning and understands our weaknesses perfectly; He is always ready “to succor his people according to their infirmities” (Alma 7:12).
Sister Tamara W. Runia taught that “the invitation to repent is an expression of God’s love. Saying yes to that invitation is an expression of ours” (“Your Repentance Doesn’t Burden Jesus Christ; It Brightens His Joy,”, May 2025, 91).
I testify that today can be a new day and tomorrow will be a better day for all who come unto Jesus Christ and receive His light in their lives. He lovingly beckons, “Come unto me, … and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Paul H. Sinclair
title: Quick to Help, Slow to Judge
content:
The Parable of the Baffling Buttons

“And a little child shall lead them.” Some years ago, this scripture truly came alive to me. It happened during a ward Primary program.
That Sabbath morning, my young friend James was wearing a new suit. As the program began, James was examining some of the more interesting aspects of his new suit. What most captured his attention were two features of his jacket. On his jacket sleeves there were buttons but no holes. And on the left lapel of his jacket there was a buttonhole but no buttons. Neither the buttons nor the buttonhole seemed to be serving any real purpose.
Well, James cleverly devised a purpose for both. I anxiously watched as James delightedly buttoned his right sleeve to his left jacket lapel. Being pleased with himself quickly gave way to being panicked, because once James had buttoned his arm to his chest, even with the flexibility of a Primary child, he could not get himself loose. James had unintentionally, but quite successfully, created a one-arm straitjacket.
As James became more and more stuck, I became more and more aggravated. Baffling buttons had been put to an uncomfortable and, to me, irritating purpose. I was shaking my head in disappointment as James was about to go to the pulpit.
Just then I noticed the little girl sitting next to James. She had also witnessed James’s predicament and his growing concern. But instead of being aggravated, she wanted to help. Quickly discerning what action was needed, she reached up with her tiny, nonjudgmental fingers and popped the button out of the buttonhole. James was rescued, and the Primary program was saved!
I felt relieved but also humbled. I recognized the quiet rebuke of a misplaced button and tiny fingers reminding me that I should be trying to be more like Jesus. That small but majestic moment helped me embrace what Elder Patrick Kearon has described as “a radical reorientation” of my soul. I don’t recall the topic of the Primary program that day, but the message I received through the Holy Ghost prompted a spiritual realignment. A little child led me to learn this: that a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge.

The Savior Helps (and Does Not Judge) the Woman at the Well

The Savior taught this loving principle of discipleship from the very beginning of His mortal ministry. In the Gospel of John, He ministers to a Samaritan woman. We do not know her name. We have come to know her as “the woman at the well.” Her interaction with the Lord Jesus Christ teaches many lessons. One critical lesson is the example of the Savior being quick to offer grace and transformative help.
As the conversation opened, Jesus was weary and unexpectedly asked the woman for a drink. We can only imagine how many days this woman had been coming to this well at this hour, alone—until this day. To her, it was an ordinary day—until Jesus showed up. In her ordinary days, she may have endured many judging eyes but few helping hands—until this day.
This woman may have done more to warrant judgment than merely buttoning her sleeve to her lapel. Apparently, she had a series of broken relationships and was, at that moment, living with a man who was not her husband. But what do we actually know about her circumstances? Was she widowed? divorced? abandoned? We do not know. Now, please don’t misunderstand me. Her story is very important, but these are not the judgmental details we need to know about her journey.
What did Christ focus on instead? Help. The offer of “living water.” The Great Redeemer of all knew absolutely everything about this unnamed woman, and He came to her to be a living witness of living water. He offered her grace and transformative help.
He spoke to the woman with dignity, not shame. He earnestly listened to her questions and responded with teaching, not ridicule. He did not hold her hostage to her history. He trusted her with truth. Jesus Christ reminds us that to help people transform their lives, we must look not only to their past—we must look to their possible. She walked to the well that day as a pariah. She walked away from the well with a purpose. That is precisely what “quick to help and slow to judge” looks like.

Showing Up on the Ordinary Days of Friends and New Members

Every day, missionaries meet people at modern-day wells all around the world. They declare that Jesus is the Christ, the great “I Am.” They find, teach, baptize, and confirm people who may be in fear of judgment but in need of help. As disciples of Jesus Christ, we are invited to reorient our souls so we may help friends and new members in more Christlike ways. President Dallin H. Oaks has plainly and directly invited us to “seek to be holy, like our Savior.” Being quick to help and slow to judge is a simple and deeply encouraging way for each of us to be more holy, to be more like our Savior, to be His true disciples.
I pray that when these modern-day men and women at the well meet you and me, they will know they have “come home.” I pray they will recognize in you and me striving disciples of Jesus Christ, ready to fill them with living and loving water. I testify that when we help people, one by one, in our own small and simple ways, rather than judge them, we are preparing the world for the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. I so witness and testify in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Gary E. Stevenson
title: Fruit to Make One Happy
content:
Introduction

I have come to expect something when I am on the Lord’s errand. Why? Because it happens every time I travel. I meet remarkable, extraordinary people, Latter-day Saints and friends. I am always impressed with children I meet. Primary children! Everywhere, most recently in Australia, New Caledonia, Samoa, Colombia, and Peru. Sometimes you even draw our pictures, and you always improve how I look!

When we speak in conference, we speak to everyone, but some of my message today will be more directly to you, children of Primary age. You know who you are—some watching from home and others in a Church building. As this is the last conference session, you may be tired or restless. I remember, when I was your age, my mother saying, many times, “Gary, pay attention and listen. Just one more talk.”
I know you have a purpose. “Your Heavenly Father and His Son, Jesus Christ, know you and love you.” Even though you are young, “you are an important part of Their work.” You are some of the most valued and faithful members of the whole Church. You can help to make your homes, your communities, and even the world better. You are our future. I feel so happy when I attend Primary and listen to your talks, your answers to gospel questions, and to hear you sing. “Heavenly Father has given you talents and spiritual gifts. He wants you to use these gifts and talents to be happy and bless others.”

Fruit to Make One Happy

When I was young like you, I loved fruit—and our family tradition of buying fresh fruit from farm stands during harvest. One stand was known for its delicious peaches. They were so sweet and juicy. Somehow, apples, cherries, and apricots bought from the farmer where they were grown seemed sweeter. Here I am with my dad next to a fruit display. Even today I love seeing and tasting delicious and unique fruits from your countries.

Now that we are all hungry, let us read a Book of Mormon story. Do you remember the prophet Lehi’s vision? He was drawn to a magnificent tree and its fruit. Lehi reflected, “I beheld a tree, whose fruit was desirable to make one happy.” He exclaimed that “it was most sweet, above all that I ever before tasted.” It filled his “soul with exceedingly great joy.”

The tree stands for the love of God, including the greatest manifestations of that love: the birth, life, and atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ. The fruit symbolizes blessings received through the Atonement of Jesus Christ, including ordinances, covenants, and truths of the restored gospel and ultimately eternal life.

Think for a moment about your favorite fruits. Are they pineapples, bananas, and grapes? Or mangoes, strawberries, and coconuts? We can hold the fruit, feel it, and look at it. We might smell it and guess how sweet it is. But once we have tasted it, we know how much we like it. Gospel truths are the same. We learn them at home, Primary, and through the scriptures. They become sweet to us as we live them, bringing us happiness and joy. Let me share three fruits of the gospel that I love.

Children of a Loving Heavenly Father

First, we are children of a loving Heavenly Father. Latter-day Saints know that we “once lived with Heavenly Father, who knows everything and loves everyone.” We are His children. Heavenly Father knows us personally. This is your most important identity. “He wants you to be like Him! He gave you a body, abilities, and spiritual gifts. He wants you and all of His children to discover and develop these gifts. He gave us a plan to help us be happy and bless others.” Having this knowledge makes us stronger. This knowledge also makes us kinder to others, knowing that everyone around us is our brother or sister.

I am so grateful that you share this fruit with others when you sing our beloved song found in the “I Am a Child of God.” Recently, I conducted a devotional with members in South America. Many were suffering because of a severe earthquake they had experienced. As I invited Primary children to stand and all to sing “I Am a Child of God,” out of the congregation, an incredibly young Primary boy got away from his parents and ran right up to the stand next to me. As I swooped him up, he sang every word of the Primary song in his sweet, loud, young voice. This testimony was so important and powerful, inviting the Spirit to comfort and testify to all that we are children of a loving Heavenly Father, even in the most difficult of times.
The Apostle Paul in the New Testament taught, “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.”

The Great Plan of Happiness Through Jesus Christ

Second, the great plan of happiness through Jesus Christ. When I lived in Japan, I became friends with a Buddhist temple priest. He was a happy man. But when his wife died, leaving him alone, he became incredibly sad, even depressed. One night a friend and I visited him at his temple to minister to him. At first, he was reluctant to talk, so grief-stricken and inconsolable. When I asked him if he knew where his wife was, he at once lifted his head, startled at the question. “What do you mean?”
We shared with him that the spirits of all men and women, when they pass away, “are taken home to that God who gave them life” and that in God’s loving plan for His children, the spirit of this man’s beloved wife, an honorable woman, was received into a place called the spirit world, where she could enter a state of rest, happiness, and peace. His countenance changed in that moment. It was as if we watched him partake of the fruit of the tree of life and his soul was filled “with exceedingly great joy.” We witnessed a miraculous transformation: peace for despair, joy for sadness, hope for ashes.
The Book of Mormon calls this “the great plan of happiness.” Central to this plan is the Atonement of Jesus Christ.
This is why Jesus Christ is the strength of youth. “He has done everything necessary for you”—for us—“to have joy in this life and forever.” Even when we make mistakes and feel discouraged or wonder if we will ever be good enough, “there is good news—wonderful, hopeful news! Because God loves [us], He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who took upon Himself [our] sins so [we] can repent, be forgiven, and keep progressing.”
I find no greater testimony that captures the great plan of happiness than when Primary children worldwide sing, “Gethsemane! Jesus loves me,” from a new hymn that we love.

The Gift of the Holy Ghost

Finally, a most delicious fruit for Latter-day Saints is the gift of the Holy Ghost, His constant companionship. When you turn eight years old, following your baptism, you receive this gift by the laying on of hands. Hundreds of thousands of recent converts have also been confirmed and received the Holy Ghost.
We know through revelation the Holy Ghost “is a personage of Spirit” and a member of the Godhead. His very important roles include to warn, to comfort, and to testify. A Primary song you often sing, “I Know My Father Lives,” teaches this: “I know my Father lives and loves me too. The Spirit whispers this to me and tells me it is true, and tells me it is true.”

Conclusion

To my young friends, you have been exceptionally good listeners as I illustrated three delicious fruits of the gospel: we are children of a loving Heavenly Father, the great plan of happiness through Jesus Christ, and the gift of the Holy Ghost.
I close by extending an invitation. When Lehi partook of the fruit in his dream, he said, “It filled my soul with exceedingly great joy; wherefore, I began to be desirous that my family should partake of it also.” He invited his family to eat the delicious fruit with him. Similarly, consider how your family, friends, and loved ones will be blessed to partake of the fruit that blesses you.
I invite you to do something that is as simple as gospel fruit is delicious: love, share, and invite. Do this with words and actions. As you do so, I promise that you will not only feel joy and happiness that comes as you partake of fruit of the gospel but even greater joy as loved ones around you partake as well.
I close with my testimony of God the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost and of Jesus Christ as our Savior and Redeemer. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Gabriel W. Reid
title: You Are Good Enough to Teach
content:
Shortly after I was sustained as a member of the Sunday School General Presidency, I felt inadequate, overwhelmed, and completely out of place.
I realized later that I was not the only one trying to make sense of it because I saw a news headline that read, “New Sunday School Leaders Include Men Involved in Church Education and an NFL Player.”
Each time I read the headline, I smile and think, “Thankfully, that headline didn’t share the names because I really hope people think I’m one of the scholars!” I especially feel that way today.
Although the headline makes me laugh, it does not always quiet this feeling inside of me: “Lord, I love You, but do You really have the right person?”
Perhaps you have asked yourself similar questions:
Do I know enough?
Am I good enough to teach the gospel of Jesus Christ?
As I have reflected on the Savior, the Master Teacher, I have noticed a beautiful pattern. Often, as He invited someone to teach His gospel, He also gave them a promise.
To a small group of ordinary fishermen on the shores of Galilee, men with willing hearts but little experience, He said, “Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men.” He did not expect them to become master teachers before they followed Him. He promised that He would make them into who He needed them to be.
In the Book of Mormon: Another Testament of Jesus Christ, the sons of Mosiah were still young when they went to teach the gospel to the Lamanites. Their past was marked by rebellion, yet their hearts had been changed through the Savior’s redeeming power. As they desired to teach their brethren, the Lord promised, “I will make an instrument of thee in my hands.”
The Lord invites all of us to teach His gospel. Wherever we teach—in classrooms, in the mission field, in our homes, or one by one—His promise remains the same: He will help us do His work.
