We were never meant to do His work alone.
Before the Savior taught His disciples where to go and what to teach, He taught them who to become. His first lesson was not about teaching—it was about discipleship.
And at the heart of discipleship and all that He does is love.
When asked which commandment was the greatest, the Savior taught, first, to love the Lord our God with all our heart, soul, and mind and, second, to love our neighbor as ourselves.
For every gospel teacher, for every disciple, these two great commandments become one simple invitation: Love the Lord and love those you teach.

My first gospel teachers were my parents. Our home in the village of Leone, American Samoa, became my first classroom of gospel learning. Under one roof, 13 children, two faithful parents, and often extended family learned and lived the gospel together.
My father joined the Church as a young man. My mother had limited formal education. But together they possessed something far more important: a deep and abiding faith in Jesus Christ. They loved the Lord with all their hearts, and because they loved Him, they loved us in a way that helped us love Him too.
Some of the greatest lessons they taught were the ones we caught simply by watching them.
Those truths were lovingly reinforced by faithful teachers in this little village chapel.

Many of my earliest Primary classes were held beneath the shade of a mango tree.
Our teachers faithfully prepared each lesson, but what I remember most is how they loved us. They knew us personally—even by name. Their love helped us feel the Savior’s love, and feeling His love helped us feel the truth of His gospel. Looking back, I realize my parents and my Church teachers were following the pattern of the Master Teacher.
The impact of a gospel teacher is not just the message—it is the love of the messenger.

My wife and I will always cherish our time in the Australia Sydney Mission. We fell in love with the wonderful people of Sydney and were blessed to serve alongside more than 500 missionaries from over 30 countries.
We learned that the surest way to truly love those we taught was to deepen our love for the One we taught about. As our love for the Savior deepened, He taught us to see the missionaries as He sees them and to love them as He loves them.
When the resurrected Savior appeared to the people in the Americas, He did not begin by delivering a sermon to the multitude. He began by focusing on the individuals. He invited each person to come unto Him one by one so they could know for themselves that He was Jesus Christ.
Only then did He teach them His doctrine and the ordinances of His gospel.
Later, after teaching many other precious truths, Jesus invited the people to return home and ponder what they had learned. We may say that “class” had ended, but His love for the people had not. When He perceived the desire of their hearts, He was filled with compassion. He healed their sick, blessed their children, and prayed for them one by one.
For the Master Teacher, every lesson was inspired by love for those He taught.
Christ-centered teaching is rooted in relationships. The inspired new Sunday schedule offers weekly opportunities to know and love those we teach, helping them come closer to the Savior and helping them deepen their conversion.
That is His pattern for every gospel lesson—even shorter ones.
Some may ask, “How can I teach everything in 25 minutes?”
Perhaps the better question is “How can I help those I teach connect to the Savior sooner?”
President Dallin H. Oaks taught, “A gospel teacher will never obscure [a learner’s] view of the Master by standing in the way.”
The purpose of every lesson is not for people to leave talking about the teacher. It is for them to leave thinking about and loving the Savior.
Twenty-five-minute lessons are not a limitation; they are an invitation: to focus, more clearly than ever, on helping others come to the Savior.
If class members leave the lesson feeling closer to the Savior than when they came, we have taught enough.
Brothers and sisters, if you are wondering whether you are good enough to teach the gospel of Jesus Christ, the answer is yes!
Not because you know everything.
Not because you have every teaching skill.
Not because you always feel capable or confident.
Because you can love the Master Teacher!
And as you deepen your love for the One you teach about, He will teach you, walk beside you, and gradually make you into the teacher He knows you can become.
Whether you see yourself as a scholar, an athlete, a lifelong disciple, or someone who has recently started—or started again—to follow Christ, the invitation is the same.

Come unto the Master Teacher. Learn of Him. Love Him. As you do, He will help you love those you teach—and that love will make your teaching more like His.
To teach like the Savior, we must love like the Savior!
This is my prayer and invitation, in the name of the Master Teacher, whom we love and who loved us first, even Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Clark G. Gilbert
title: Teach Truth with Love
content:
Introduction

It takes courage to stand for truth. It takes even more courage to stand for truth with love. President Dallin H. Oaks has repeatedly emphasized this message. Last general conference he explained the challenge: “When we seek to keep all the commandments in our personal lives, we are sometimes accused of having no love for those who don’t. When we show personal love and support loving causes, we are sometimes misunderstood as implying support for results that contradict our … religious duties.”
In preparing my message today, I have worried that some would selectively anchor only on truth or others would only anchor on love. I also worried some would see only others’ shortcomings and forget their own weaknesses. I remember when President Russell M. Nelson gave his talk on peacemaking, I started a mental list of everyone I thought needed his message. He then gave this caution: “You may be thinking … this message would really help someone [else] you know. … But I also hope that you will look deeply into your [own] heart to see if there are shards of pride or jealousy that prevent you from becoming a peacemaker.”
I extend that same invitation to all of us today.

Five Principles in Standing for Truth with Love

Several years ago I received an assignment to speak at Ensign College. President Oaks was the main devotional speaker, and he asked that I speak with him on some of the challenging doctrinal topics of the day. This was a daunting assignment. He then suggested that we not use formal written remarks. Now, I know we follow the prophet, but I hesitantly, even sheepishly, replied that for the sake of the Church, maybe we should write out at least what I said. He relented, and the devotional was entitled “Stand Fast with Love in Proclaiming Truth.” In the address, President Oaks shared five principles I have felt impressed to amplify today.

Principle 1: Avoid Overly Contentious Settings

First, avoid overly contentious settings. Elder Neil L. Andersen stated, “There are times when being a peacemaker means that we resist the impulse to respond and instead, with dignity, remain quiet.”
Consider Dostoevsky’s literary description of Christ and the Grand Inquisitor. After repeatedly being denounced, the Savior simply kissed His accuser with no further response. In a lesser way, I recently felt this when a group of national academic leaders aggressively criticized the role of faith in higher education. Recognizing the escalating tension of the moment, I chose at least for that setting to table the discussion despite my strong disagreement with what was being said.
Sometimes tense moments make it more difficult to see what is really causing someone’s protestations. President Nelson taught: “If friends and family should step away from the Church, continue to love them. … Do not be led astray by those whose doubts may be fueled by things you cannot see in their lives.” I think of Sister Anette Dennis’s story of the wounded dog who uncharacteristically wouldn’t respond to her owner. Sometimes what we perceive as hostility may actually be someone’s hidden pain or regret.
I failed to see this with a friend who had at one time been spiritually faithful but was now attacking the Church. My frustration came not just because of his bitterness but because I knew he knew better. Unfortunately, rather than recognize the tension of the moment or that he might be hurting for reasons I could not see, I shot back an angry retort. I may have won the debate in the moment, but I lost the Spirit and I failed to help my struggling friend. That day I stood for truth, but I did it without love and without charity.

Principle 2: Find Common Ground

A second way to stand for truth with love is to first find common ground. A stake president once brought me a long list of ministering visits. I suggested he choose just one home, given our schedule limitations. Technically he honored the request. But when we arrived at the home, there were five separate individuals waiting inside, each with a completely different concern. I asked, “Well, where do you want to start?” As I listened to their stories, I was tempted at times to interject, but the Spirit kept prompting me to wait. After nearly two hours of listening, going right through our next meeting, I began to better understand their struggles and I could feel their heartfelt strivings. And when I invited them to come to stake conference that evening, each one of them accepted.
Resisting the impulse to initially respond built common ground, which allowed me later to teach from a place of love. As with the Savior, “we love him, because he [loved us first].”

Principle 3: Be a Light

The third principle is to be a light. President Nelson taught: “Let your skeptical friends see how much you love the Lord and His gospel. Surprise their doubting hearts with your believing heart!” The best way to help someone else keep their covenants is to keep your covenants. As Sister Tamara Runia reminded us, “Stay at the tree, … continue to beckon to those you love … that eating the fruit is a happy thing!”
I shared earlier the story of a tense setting with academic leaders. Perhaps in part because I chose not to engage in the moment, later a university chancellor reached out for counsel in creating a course on character at one of the nation’s most prestigious academic institutions. Being a light opens more doors than any pointed argument ever will.

Principle 4: Hold to Truth Even in Our Outreach

Now, the fourth principle is to hold to truth even in our outreach. In April, President Oaks stated that showing love for others “does not mean surrendering our values. The covenants we have made inevitably position us as devoted participants in the eternal contest between truth and error.”
President Jeffrey R. Holland similarly reminded us, “Jesus clearly understood what many in our modern culture seem to forget: that there is a crucial difference between the commandment to forgive sin (which He had an infinite capacity to do) and the warning against condoning it (which He never ever did even once).”
President Holland simplified this further when he stated, “As near as I can tell, Christ never once withheld His love from anyone, but He also never once said to anyone, ‘Because I love you, you are exempt from keeping my commandments.’”
Some have argued that loving our neighbor (the second commandment) somehow supersedes or takes priority over loving God (the first commandment). But President D. Todd Christofferson pointed out: “Putting the first commandment first does not diminish or limit our ability to keep the second commandment. To the contrary, it amplifies and strengthens it. … Our love of God elevates our ability to love others more fully and perfectly because we in essence partner with God in the care of His children.”
When we try to love others by minimizing God’s laws, we separate ourselves from the one person who loves them the very most. The Savior showed love for the woman taken in adultery. But He also charged her to “go, and sin no more.”

Principle 5: Stay Anchored in Jesus Christ

President Nelson cautioned that the “messages [of the adversary] tend to be loud, bold, and boastful,” while Heavenly Father communicates “simply, quietly, and with such stunning plainness that we cannot misunderstand.” Christ modeled this perfectly for us.
The fifth principle then is to stay anchored in Jesus Christ. Ask yourself if you carry these Christlike attributes when you are striving to stand for truth with love: “And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in … truth.”

Closing

For disciples of Jesus Christ, truth and love always walk together. I believe teaching truth with love will be the hallmark of Christ’s disciples in the last days. For some this will require greater conviction. For others it will demand greater charity. I know the Lord will help us as we strive to teach truth with love. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

speaker: Dallin H. Oaks
title: Closing Remarks
content:
My dear brothers and sisters, the great messages of this conference and the Spirit of the Lord have inspired all of us to concentrate our worship, focus our learning, and unite our testimonies on the teachings of the Lord Jesus Christ and His Father’s plan for our eternal increase and joy.
As the talks of this conference are published, we invite all to study and ponder them prayerfully and to act in faith on the principles they explain. The Lord has promised, “Unto him that receiveth I will give more.”
As we look forward, we are welcoming the world, in person or virtually, to the Salt Lake Temple Celebration. On April 5, 2027, the temple doors will open to the public—the first such opening since 1893, 134 years ago.
Join us at TempleSquare.org or through the Temple Square app to learn more.
Following this session of general conference, the first episode of a dynamic video series,, will premiere worldwide in multiple languages. More will come in the months ahead, including a virtual tour of the Salt Lake Temple.
As we now go forward, we invoke the blessings of the Lord on you and your families, blessings of peace and contentment. And we bless your service of the Lord Jesus Christ in these challenging times.
I close with my testimony. This is the restored gospel of Jesus Christ in His Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Truth is to be found here—truth about the teachings of the Lord and truth about the covenant path that will lead us to our destiny, the destiny desired by our Heavenly Father. Of all this I testify to you in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
